articles.title: Police probe ‘terror’ incident near RAF base used in Iran war: What we know
articles.summary: Five men were arrested on suspicion of the ‘preparation of a terrorist act’ near RAF Fairford, a base used by the US.
articles.body:
British security officials are exploring “multiple lines of enquiry” following the arrest of five men on Sunday morning on suspicion of the “preparation of a terrorist act” near a British Royal Air Force (RAF) base in southern England that has been used by the United States in various conflicts.

Armed officers arrested the group of men after calls from residents to emergency services reported three “suspicious vehicles which appeared to be travelling towards the air base”, London’s Metropolitan Police said in a statement.

“Counter Terrorism Policing can now confirm they are leading an investigation into an incident which took place overnight near RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire,” the police added.

Later, in a statement on Monday, the counterterrorism police said the five arrested men were all British nationals aged between 23 and 25.

Calling the incident “deeply concerning”, United Kingdom Prime Minister Andy Burnham said his government would take “every step necessary” to protect the public.

Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said on Monday the incident was “a reminder of the threats our country faces”.

“I want to thank our security services, armed forces and police for the work they did yesterday and they do all year round to help keep our country safe,” he said, addressing a crowd in Liverpool at the Labour Party conference. “We will always stand up for our security against those who would do us harm.”

He said the UK must be prepared to “confront” all security threats facing Europe and the world, adding: “We will act against the proxies of Iran.”

Iran, however, rejected suggestions of its involvement, describing them as “fabricated speculations” aimed at fuelling “Iranophobia propaganda in the UK”.

Based in Gloucestershire, RAF Fairford is a British military base that hosts the United States Air Force’s 501st Combat Support Wing.

It is one of 12 UK bases, including RAF Lakenheath, which hosts the largest US force group in the UK, and RAF Mildenhall, which supports refuelling and global operations.

The Fairford base was also used by US forces during their attacks on Iran amid the ongoing conflict, during which they deployed B-1 and B-2 bombers from the facility.

In March, then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer granted permission for “defensive” US action against Iranian missile sites from two UK bases, including Fairford and Diego Garcia, in the British Indian Ocean Territory.

On Sunday, Gloucestershire police said they received a call about “three suspicious vehicles” travelling towards the base at 00:45 local time (23:45 GMT on Saturday).

Broadcast aerial footage showed a bomb disposal robot moving around the vans, two of which had their rear doors open.

Police believed the incident had been “contained” and put a 400-metre (1,300-foot) cordon in place.

A farmer who called 999 told BBC Radio 4 on condition of anonymity that she arrived home in the nearby village of Whelford to find the driveway blocked and saw a “large group of hooded and masked men”.

“When they saw me, they ran ahead of me – some into the field and some towards the neighbouring village of Kempsford. I then realised that something highly unusual was taking place,” she added.

The woman told the BBC that she called the Ministry of Defence police at the airbase, but there was no answer; after calling 999 at 01:36 BST (00:36 GMT), she said, “within 10 minutes the village was full of armed police”.

“I am absolutely staggered that it was left to me as a member of the public to see and report this,” she said, adding: “Someone really dropped the ball on this.”

About 85 households in the nearby village of Whelford were advised to evacuate. Those residents also spoke of “heightened tensions” in the area in recent weeks with frequent police patrols.

The counterterrorism police have since taken over the investigation.

In their statement on Monday, the counterterrorism police identified the arrested men as London residents: a 24-year-old from Camden, a 24-year-old from Westminster, a 25-year-old from Westminster, a 23-year-old from Westminster and a 24-year-old from Willesden.

The five were arrested in Whelford on Sunday morning, the counterterrorism police said, on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act and the “preparation of a terrorist act”.

The men remain in custody, and police have not disclosed where they are being kept.

When asked whether police were looking for more suspects in connection with the incident, Maggie Blyth, the temporary chief constable of Gloucestershire police, said she believed it was “contained”.

Still, the counterterrorism police statement said, “the nature of this investigation means significant numbers of resources, including military assets, remain deployed at the location” in reference to the region around Whelford and RAF Fairford. “We are working hard to minimise disruption to local communities, but ask for their patience, as our work continues at the scene.”

The cordon around the area remains in place, the statement added.

US President Donald Trump said on Sunday that the suspects were “looking to do big damage” at the airbase.

“We had them under view for a long time, and we got them,” he said, adding the US and the UK had been working together on the incident.

Rob Geist Pinfold, an international security lecturer at King’s College London, explained that under British law the identity of the men would not be disclosed unless they were charged.

“We don’t know anything about whether they’re British nationals, whether they’re foreign nationals, for example. And we also don’t know what was in those vans,” Pinfold told Al Jazeera.

“Trump’s statement there suggests these men were under investigation as well. So, we don’t know how much of this is simply a member of the public spotting something suspicious that sounds pretty inept or whether this is some sort of well-planned and poorly executed attempt to cause damage at Fairford,” he added.

The Iranian embassy in the UK, in a statement on X, rejected any link with the men arrested for the alleged plot to target RAF Fairford.

“The Embassy of the Islamic Republic of Iran in London categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations published by some British individuals and media outlets attempting to link Iran to arrest of five suspects in the vicinity of RAF Fairford base,” the embassy said, before referring to the US and Israeli war on Iran to paint the country as a victim of foreign aggression.

Are British authorities linking Iran to the incident?

They are not — but they haven’t ruled it out yet either.

Tehran has previously said it would target US military bases that had launched attacks on Iran.

Since February 28, when the US and Israel first launched their strikes on Iran, Tehran has targeted multiple military bases in the Gulf and the broader Middle East, including those in Qatar, Bahrain, Jordan, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Iraq, Oman and the United Arab Emirates. In early March, a loitering munition also struck an RAF base in Cyprus, where authorities claimed Iranian drones aimed at the base were also intercepted.

Secretary of State for Defence Wes Streeting said on Sunday he had been in contact with US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and the UK was “working closely with our American friends”.

When asked whether Iran was involved, he said it would be “irresponsible to speculate”.

British police have been cautious about attributing motive or responsibility for the foiled plot.

“This is a hugely complex and large-scale operation, involving local and national policing, the MOD, and local agencies, who are working together to progress the investigation and support for the community,” Vicki Evans, senior national coordinator for counterterrorism police, said in a statement.

“I am very aware of the levels of speculation about the motivation behind this incident, and the geopolitical questions that are being raised. However, I ask that at this time, CTP are given the space to work carefully and clearly.”

What are the inconsistencies about the details behind the foiled plot?

On Monday morning, Streeting thanked the resident who spoke to the BBC about reporting the masked men near the airbase, saying, “She has done exactly what we would hope that someone in that extraordinary situation would do.”

“With respect, though, she does only have a partial picture. And that’s as far as I wish to go this morning,” he said, without elaborating.

Moreover, Trump’s comments that the suspects had been under watch raise questions about how the masked men were able to get so close to the airbase and why they were foiled by a resident purely by chance.

articles.title: Mapping Israel’s 300 checkpoints: Where they are and how they work
articles.summary: Israel has shut occupied West Bank crossings for a week, further restricting Palestinian movement and holy site access.
articles.body:
Israel has sealed off the occupied West Bank for a week, shutting its crossings and tightening restrictions on Palestinian movement, citing the Jewish holiday of Sukkot.

Defence Minister Israel Katz on Sunday ordered the closure on the military’s recommendation, and it will remain in place until Saturday.

Palestinians already face severe restrictions on their movement due to hundreds of Israeli checkpoints and barriers across the occupied territory. Now, controls at checkpoints and barriers across the territory will tighten further, cutting off access to holy sites such as the Al-Aqsa Mosque in occupied East Jerusalem and the Ibrahimi Mosque in Hebron in the West Bank.

In the Ramallah and el-Bireh governorate on Sunday, Israeli forces blocked roads and shut the entrances to Turmus Aya, Aboud, Nabi Saleh, Atara and Taybeh. In Yabroud, Ein Siniya and Jaba, soldiers set up checkpoints to search vehicles and check IDs.

The closure also bars Palestinians who still hold permits to work in Israel and its settlements, a workforce already sharply reduced since Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza began in October 2023. Only workers deemed essential are allowed into Israeli industrial zones in the West Bank.

For decades, Palestinians in the West Bank have looked for work inside Israel because of high unemployment and low wages at home, which are the result of nearly six decades of Israeli occupation that has restricted their economy, land and movement.

The United Nations General Assembly passed a resolution in September 2024 calling on Israel to end its “unlawful” occupation within a year. Israel has since doubled down, intensifying raids on Palestinians, deploying soldiers with settlers during their increasing attacks on Palestinian towns and expanding its settlements, which are illegal under international law.

Before the war on Gaza began, about 160,000 Palestinians from the West Bank worked for Israeli employers, most of them inside Israel and the rest in settlements, according to the Palestinian Institute for Economic Policy Research .

After Israel barred most permit holders from entering, that number fell to about 27,300, by mid-2024. Unemployment in the West Bank rose from 12.9 percent in September 2023 to 30.7 percent a year later, according to the Israeli rights group Gisha .

There are more than 300 Israeli checkpoints across the West Bank, according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs. As of December, they were among 925 obstacles restricting the movement of 3.4 million Palestinians across the West Bank and East Jerusalem. They are:

218 partial checkpoints staffed intermittently, 152 of which have gates (90 usually open and 62 frequently closed)

232 road gates , 159 of them frequently closed

114 linear closures , such as earth walls, road barriers and trenches

For Palestinians in the West Bank, these checkpoints cut off or restrict access between towns and main roads, forcing hundreds of thousands of people onto longer routes to work and school. They also hinder access to medical care.

Qalandiya checkpoint : The main crossing between Ramallah and East Jerusalem once handled about a third of all movement between the West Bank and Israel.

Checkpoint 300 : It blocks the road between Bethlehem and Jerusalem and is the main route for Palestinians working in East Jerusalem and other central cities.

Eyal checkpoint : It serves workers from Qalqilya, where Israel’s separation wall has driven up unemployment, and from across the northern West Bank.

Taybeh checkpoint : It lies just south of the northern Palestinian city of Tulkarem.

Tarqumiyah checkpoint: It is near Hebron in the southern West Bank.

articles.title: Trump’s Greenland bases could change Arctic defense. I learned why at 76 below zero
articles.summary: Trump's Greenland deal expands Arctic Ocean defense, but a veteran of 76-below-zero Alaska warns that cold-weather bases demand far more.
articles.body: I spent four years as an Army infantry officer in Alaska, where our operational responsibilities stretched from Prudhoe Bay on the Arctic Ocean to the Aleutian Islands reaching toward Russia. During Exercise Brim Frost ’89, some 26,000 American and Canadian troops took the field, and I served as a brigade operations officer. As we maneuvered across Alaska’s interior, temperatures plunged as low as 76 degrees below zero. The exercise produced more than 250 cold-weather injuries, including 88 cases of frostbite. At those temperatures, fuel systems become unreliable, batteries lose power, lubricants thicken, and weapons and vehicles can fail in ways soldiers from warmer climates rarely encounter. And no, a week on the slopes at Vail does not prepare anyone for that. The Arctic punishes amateurs. TRUMP’S GREENLAND DEAL SET FOR SIGNING AFTER MONTHS-LONG FIGHT OVER US CONTROL That experience is why President Donald Trump’s Greenland announcement at the United Nations on Tuesday deserves attention beyond the political headlines. "We’ll be building two very major military bases," the president told the General Assembly. The agreement Trump signed with Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenland Premier Jens-Frederik Nielsen amends the 1951 defense pact. It allows the United States to modernize and expand the existing Pituffik Space Base in the northwest and to establish new defense areas at Narsarsuaq in the south and Mestersvig in the northeast. It also grants U.S. forces broad access by land, air and sea, including undersea access for American public vessels within Greenland’s territorial waters. TRUMP DECLARES VICTORY IN HISTORIC DEAL WITH GREENLAND AS HE SECURES 'PERMANENT' US MILITARY RIGHTS Announcing an Arctic base, however, is a long way from making one operational. Frederiksen said no decision has been made on the specifics of Golden Dome, and Washington has yet to say which forces will occupy the new sites or when. Forget the flat map and look at the globe from over the North Pole. Alaska, northern Canada and Greenland form the northern approaches to North America, and Greenland sits astride the routes connecting the Arctic Ocean, the North Atlantic and Europe. WHY TRUMP ZEROED IN ON GREENLAND, THE WORLD’S LARGEST ISLAND, MOSTLY COVERED IN ICE — IN 3 CHARTS The Pentagon’s 2024 Arctic Strategy calls the North American Arctic vital to homeland defense because it hosts NORAD’s aerospace and maritime warning. Greenland has been strategic terrain for generations. Narsarsuaq itself was an American air base, Bluie West One, until the United States closed it in 1958. At the height of the Cold War, Washington operated 17 military facilities with more than 10,000 troops on the island. Today only Pituffik remains, with about 150 service members. TRUMP’S MASSIVE GREENLAND DEAL MAKES CLEAR WHO CONTROLS THE ARCTIC’S STRATEGIC FUTURE Pituffik supports missile warning, missile defense and space surveillance. The new agreement recognizes American access to defend Greenland, the NATO area and the American continent, including through the Golden Dome, Trump’s planned missile-defense system. Add Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig, and the United States could build a distributed Arctic network. Pituffik is already the northern sensor and space node. Narsarsuaq could strengthen access to Greenland’s southern approaches and the North Atlantic, while Mestersvig could extend American and allied reach toward the Greenland Sea. ARCTIC POWER PLAY GIVES TOP US ADVERSARY NEW OPENING WITH RUSSIA AS US STAKES GROW That geography matters most against Russia. The Pentagon’s 2024 Arctic Strategy calls the North American Arctic vital to homeland defense because it hosts NORAD’s aerospace and maritime warning. Russia fields the most developed military presence in the Arctic. Its Kola Peninsula hosts the Northern Fleet and important strategic nuclear forces. The Pentagon warns that Russian Arctic capabilities could place the American homeland and allied territory at risk and complicate U.S. power projection. SECURITY EXPERT HAILS TRUMP'S GREENLAND PACT AS A 'BIG DEAL' ON PAR WITH ALASKA PURCHASE Russia does not have to invade Greenland for Greenland to matter. Russian submarines, long-range aircraft and missiles make the island important because of where it sits. More American sites could improve warning, surveillance, reinforcement and resilience while reducing our dependence on a single installation. China presents a different problem. Beijing is not an Arctic nation, yet it has spent years seeking influence there. The Pentagon strategy documents Chinese icebreaker operations, dual-use research and growing military cooperation with Russia. CHINA ‘WIRETAPPED RED SEA’ WITH SPY HUB 6 MILES FROM US BASE: EX PENTAGON OFFICIAL WARNS Against China, the agreement’s most consequential provision may involve no runway at all. No non-NATO country may establish a manned or unmanned military installation or maintain a persistent military presence in Greenland without the parties’ agreement. The pact also bars non-allied control of, or significant influence over, critical infrastructure, resource extraction and other sensitive sectors. It has no expiration date, and it requires Denmark and Greenland to ensure that any future independent Greenland remains in NATO and assumes the pact’s defense obligations. "No U.S. adversary will ever be permitted to establish a military presence in Greenland," Trump said. That closes one path to a Chinese foothold in the Arctic. TWO ICEBREAKERS HEADED TO ALASKA AS US COMBATS RUSSIAN, CHINESE INFLUENCE IN ARCTIC None of this changes the lesson I learned at 76 below zero. An Arctic base is a supply chain that has to survive January. And an Arctic force is more than troops flown north on short notice. The people operating those bases must know how to live, maintain equipment and perform their missions where routine mistakes quickly turn deadly. Fuel must arrive. Aircraft must fly. Vehicles must start. Communications must work. Soldiers must function outdoors without becoming cold-weather casualties. Spare parts must travel thousands of miles from America’s industrial base. The Army’s Arctic strategy says the service must "man, train, equip, and organize to win in the Arctic." The Pentagon calls for better communications above 65 degrees north, where satellite coverage thins. Pituffik and Mestersvig both sit well north of that line. Can two additional U.S. defense areas strengthen deterrence against Russia and China? They can, but concrete and runways alone deter no one. Deterrence exists when an adversary believes America and its allies can see what is coming, move forces, sustain them and respond effectively. Greenland strengthens each of those against Russia. Against China, denying military access and strategic investment may matter just as much. The agreement provides geography and access. The hard work is converting them into enduring capability. articles.title: HUD’s homelessness reforms put human lives ahead of housing bureaucracy
articles.summary: HUD reforms shift homelessness policy away from Housing First toward measuring recovery and self-sufficiency after a 27% surge in homelessness.
articles.body: On Sept. 16, the First Circuit Court of Appeals cleared the way for the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) to move forward with desperately needed reforms to the nation’s homelessness system. After months of litigation by the Homeless Industrial Complex to repeatedly block these reforms, the decision allows HUD to redefine success and fund the programs that generate the greatest success in moving the homeless toward recovery, restoration and self-sufficiency. And not a moment too soon. TRUMP WANTS TO HELP 146,000 MENTALLY ILL WHO ARE HOMELESS. DEMOCRATS WANT TO STOP HIM For more than a decade, federal homelessness policy has centered heavily on permanent housing placement, while the measures used to define and count homelessness have often obscured important differences between who is counted as homeless and who is being served through homelessness programs. Success will now be measured by whether people are getting better: recovering, working, reconnecting and reclaiming their lives. Getting here required that HUD officials confront a series of gimmicks that helped sustain the old system — promises, definitions and measures of success that painted a very different picture than what was happening on America’s streets. SEATTLE MAYOR SAYS SOBRIETY WON'T BE REQUIRED AT NEW HOMELESS SHELTER The first gimmick was in 2013 when President Barack Obama declared Housing First the predominant federal approach, promising to end homelessness in a decade by prioritizing permanent housing placement without requiring treatment, sobriety or other preconditions. The promised end never came. By 2025, despite a 151% increase in taxpayer-funded beds, homelessness surged 27% and chronic homelessness by 81% — reaching the highest levels ever recorded in our nation’s history. The problem was that we defined success as housing placements and system growth rather than recovery, self-sufficiency and restored lives. Spending soared, the system expanded and homelessness grew with it. LETITIA JAMES FACES SCRUTINY AFTER NEW YORK CITY SPENDS $81,700 PER HOMELESS PERSON AMID SHELTER SCANDALS That brings us to gimmick No. 2: housing people and then removing them from the homelessness count. HUD’s Point-in-Time count excludes people already living in taxpayer-funded permanent housing for the homeless even though roughly 83% of HUD’s homelessness resources are devoted to housing them. That exposes a fundamental contradiction: If they are no longer counted as homeless, why does the nation’s largest homelessness agency continue devoting the majority of its resources to housing them? SEATTLE CLEANED UP FOR THE WORLD CUP BUT ONLY WHILE THE WORLD WAS WATCHING, COMMENTATOR SAYS Then came another statistical sleight of hand: rapid rehousing. Success will now be measured by whether people are getting better: recovering, working, reconnecting and reclaiming their lives. HUD classified rapid rehousing as permanent housing even though its rental assistance is time-limited to 24 months. Move a family into rapid rehousing, and they disappear from the point-in-time count. Move that same family into transitional housing — which can also last up to 24 months — and they remain officially homeless. TAXPAYER-FUNDED 'METH MANSION' UNDER FIRE AS CRIME CONCERNS MOUNT AROUND HOMELESS CAMPUS Same potential 24-month horizon. Two radically different statistical outcomes. And the distinction mattered. As HUD steered communities away from transitional housing and toward rapid rehousing, HUD itself attributed declines in reported family homelessness in 2018 "largely" to that shift. FURIOUS RESIDENTS CONFRONT HOMELESS HOUSING LEADERS AS POPULAR BEACH COMMUNITY HITS BREAKING POINT Put the populations together and the picture changes dramatically: 1,456,923 Americans were either homeless or living in taxpayer-subsidized housing in 2025 — nearly twice the 745,652 captured by the headline point-in-time count. That is one of the flaws in defining success primarily through housing status: The statistic can improve the moment someone crosses into a program classified as permanent housing, long before we know whether that person has achieved lasting stability or self-sufficiency. Housing matters, but recovery, stability and self-sufficiency must be the finish line. Then there is the "chronic" definition gimmick. Under 12 years of Housing First rule, HUD has repeatedly changed how it defines and calculates chronic homelessness, making apples-to-apples comparisons across years increasingly difficult. Some changes temporarily altered who qualified as chronically homeless and therefore who appeared in federal statistics. But this year, this HUD administration did the calculation and reports chronic homelessness is 81% higher than it was in 2013. Perhaps the most consequential gimmick, however, involves homeless children and families. In 2011, HUD made the decision to apply a far narrower standard than the Congress-codified McKinney-Vento definition to identify homeless children and youth in our nation’s schools. The result is a stunning federal contradiction: a child can be officially homeless under federal law while at school, yet that same child and family is moved into the shadows under HUD’s narrow definition simply because, after losing their housing, they are sleeping on someone else’s couch or in a motel room the government is not funding. The definition disparity is staggering. And the distinction mattered. As HUD steered communities away from transitional housing and toward rapid rehousing, HUD itself attributed declines in reported family homelessness in 2018 "largely" to that shift. The Department of Education identified roughly 1.5 million homeless K–12 students in the 2023–24 school year, a number that includes only students. It does not count their parent(s), younger siblings not yet enrolled in school or other family members experiencing homelessness alongside them. Applying a conservative household adjustment suggests those students could represent more than 2.3 million Americans experiencing homelessness within families. The result is that most homeless families are excluded from HUD’s homelessness count, and those excluded families do not qualify for HUD-funded homelessness assistance. HUD simply defined them out of the system that was supposed to support them. Pushing them into the shadows will have consequences reverberate for generations. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Under the Trump administration, HUD now recognizes a basic truth: America cannot solve homelessness by narrowing definitions until millions disappear from the numbers — or by declaring success based simply on where someone sleeps. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The era of statistical gimmicks and lowered expectations must end. It is time to measure what matters: lives recovered, restored and returned to self-sufficiency. CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM MICHELE STEEB

articles.title: Home heating oil costs: Childminder facing 'severe financial burden'
articles.summary: The war in Iran is having a practical impact on people across the island as energy prices continue to climb.
articles.body:
Many households across Northern Ireland continue to be hit with high prices for home heating oil, with one woman saying there is a "severe" financial burden on childminders.

The war in Iran is having a practical impact on people across the island as energy prices continue to climb.

On 24 September, the average price of 500 litres of home heating oil in Northern Ireland was £561.83, according to the Consumer Council NI (CCNI) .

"It's a severe financial and operational burden on all registered childminders because as well as the prices of the oil, there's massive increases in the food bills, the insurance," Rachel Jeffers, from Stewartstown, County Tyrone said.

"That's all increased massively and a lot of the parents are saying if we're increasing our rates it's a financial burden on them."

Almost two-thirds of homes (62.5%) in Northern Ireland use oil for heating, the highest proportion of the UK nations.

Unlike gas or electricity the heating oil market is unregulated, so global price rises are rapidly passed through to consumers.

Alongside her six-year-old daughter and seven-year-old son, Jeffers minds one child after school hours and three children under school age all day.

She told BBC News NI the cost of her home heating oil had "doubled" since last year.

Last week, she purchased 500 litres of oil for £560. Jeffers said her tank was "not even near filled", but the price is currently too high to fill it completely.

Jeffers said she had found herself turning off her heating sooner in the day than she usually would.

During the winter months, Jeffers said she had to run the heating all day to keep the house warm for the young children.

"Through the summer we were still using it because our hot water runs off our heating oil," she said.

Jeffers has not yet had to increase her childminding fees, but it is something she has been "discussing".

"The guilt is there also because whenever you start minding, the families nearly become an extension of your family, so you're feeling for them."

She said the cost of home heating was "always on the back of your mind".

In terms of the knock-on impact the high costs are having on her own family, Jeffers said she has had to rethink whether to send her children to after school activities.

"They do piano, they do football, and you're sitting and questioning is it worth going to these?

"And then that's impacting on them and they're out and they feel like they're missing out because they're seeing their friends still going to it, but you obviously then can't afford to do everything," she said.

How much in home heating oil in Northern Ireland?

The CCNI's weekly oil price checker shows typical oil prices for 300, 500 and 900 litres and is updated every Thursday.

Raymond Gormley, head of energy at the CCNI, told BBC News NI that the cost of home heating oil was "about 80% more expensive than it was just before the war with Iran started".

"At the minute, 300 litres is about £347 and before the war began it was £202. That just shows you, that's £146 of a difference for 300 litres," Gormley said.

"It's really hard for people to find that 80% increase in such a short space of time because, as we know, budgets are hard pressed as it is," he said.

What will happen to oil prices this winter?

In short, Gormley said it "all depends on what happens in the Middle East".

"If there is peace discussions and there is sort of a truce, you'll see prices coming down, slowly be that, but they'll come down. If not, if war continues, prices will only go one way," he said.

He added that the oil prices were "really headline driven".

He said prices had "come down slightly in a week". However, he added: "As you know, prices go up a lot quicker than they come down."

Gormley is suggesting that people keep an eye on the daily oil prices.

"If you're going to wait and see if your price is going to come down, well then keep an eye on the daily prices," he said.

"And then you get to a point where you think you're going to buy, price around a few oil suppliers because there is a bit of variancy on prices there."

Applications for a Stormont scheme to give eligible households a £100 voucher towards home heating oil costs opened on 9 September .

About 340,000 lower-income households were expected to qualify for the payment which was first announced in March.

As of midday on 23 September, a total of 123,987 applications had been received by the Department for Communities.

Successful applicants for the Home Heating Oil Support Scheme expected to receive a payment card within 10 working days of applying.

The scheme will be open for applications until 31 March 2027.

It is open to households with a combined income of £30,000 or less, or those on certain benefits including pension credit and PIP.

It is expected that 75% or more of applications will be processed automatically.

However, some people will have to provide additional information to show they qualify.

articles.title: Woman Finds Mysterious Drawing in Her 1834 Home. Then She Uncovers a Dark Family Story (Exclusive)
articles.summary: Sommer Duran tells PEOPLE a mysterious attic drawing led her to uncover the tragic story of a great-great-aunt whose name covered the walls
articles.body:
Sommer Duran found one of her great-great-aunt's names written throughout the attic of her family's 1834 home, including beside a mysterious drawing of a woman

Curious about the relative she'd never known, Duran began searching census, marriage and death records along with newspaper archives

The mom has uncovered plenty of other surprises inside the nearly 200-year-old house, including animal skeletons, preserved food and a bottle containing spiders

Sommer Duran had seen one particular name again and again while exploring the attic of her family's 1834 home. Then she noticed it beside a drawing that made her want to know more.

The name belonged to one of Duran's great-great-aunts, and it was written across the attic among old dates, names and drawings left behind by generations before her, which she shared in a TikTok video. But after spotting what she describes as a "pretty graphic drawing" of a woman with her relative's name beside it, Duran couldn't stop wondering who she had been.

"That made me curious about who she was, so I started digging through census records, marriage and death records, old photographs and newspaper archives," Duran, 29, tells PEOPLE.

What she found turned a curiosity about writing on the wall into a tragic chapter of her family's history. Duran discovered that her great-great-aunt had gotten married and, only about two months later, was killed on Halloween.

Her death record lists her death as a homicide, according to Duran, who says she eventually tracked down old newspaper coverage of the case. While she can't know who created the attic drawing or what it was meant to depict, learning what happened to her relative changed the way she looked at it.

"I can't know for certain what the drawing in the attic was intended to represent, but finding out what happened to her definitely gave that graphic drawing a completely different context," she says.

It's the kind of rabbit hole Duran never expected to find herself going down when she and her husband, Antonio Duran, 27, began restoring the nearly 200-year-old house. Built by one of Sommer's ancestors in 1834, the home has remained in her family ever since, and the couple has continued finding traces of the people who lived there long before them.

The attic alone is covered in names, dates and drawings. Among them are sketches of people, a factory and an old school, which the family was eventually able to identify. In another unexpected connection between past and present, one of Duran's relatives now lives in that former school.

As the family has slowly worked its way through previously unexplored areas of the house, they've uncovered old newspapers and papers, family photographs, cassette tapes, VHS tapes, an answering machine, a Flinch card game and an assortment of old bottles and jars.

Then there are the discoveries that have been a little harder to explain.

"We've found two full animal skeletons — one in the attic and another that was actually stored inside an old lunchbox," Duran says.

Underneath the house near an old well area, she came across another find she wasn't eager to investigate further: a bottle containing spiders and what appeared to be a small bone.

"I put that one back where I found it!" she says.

The old jars scattered around the property have created their own mysteries. Duran and her family went through them hoping they might discover preserved food dating back to the 1800s, though she says they haven't been able to confidently trace any of the food that far back.

So far, they've identified what appear to be preserved tomatoes, onion bulbs and raspberries. An empty Triple L mason jar, which still has its lid, appears to date from around the 1890s to early 1900s based on its logo, Duran says.

One mystery jar even fooled them. What they initially thought might be old food appears instead to be bronze paint from around 1970.

Followers who have been watching Duran document the restoration online have joined the detective work, helping identify old orange juice, medicine and pickle jars by studying their logos, markings and shapes. Relatives have also helped Duran put names to faces and make connections as she digs further into the family's past.

That research has already uncovered another sad story. Duran learned that her great-great-aunt's sister also died young, not long after getting married, following an infection.

Still, much of what the house has revealed remains unresolved. Duran is continuing to search old records, identify relatives in family photographs and figure out how the names and objects scattered throughout the house connect to the people who once called it home.

"We're still trying to identify people in old family photographs and piece together more connections," Duran says. "Followers and relatives have helped a lot with the research."

articles.title: Restaurants lock up customers' phones as devices become the 'new cigarettes'
articles.summary: Locked pouches, free wine bottles and no-Wi-Fi policies are how bars and restaurants are pushing back against phones at the dinner table.
articles.body: Cigarette smoke may be gone from restaurant dining rooms, but some owners say a new distraction is affecting the experience: customers glued to their phones. Bars and restaurants are finding increasingly creative ways to get diners to focus more on the experience and less on their screens, from locked pouches like those used in schools to a free bottle of wine. At Antagonist, a cocktail bar in Charlotte, North Carolina, guests receive a lockable pouch for their phones upon entry — one example of devices becoming the "new cigarettes" in restaurants, as The Wall Street Journal recently put it. RESTAURANTS BAN DINERS' PHONES DURING MEALS AS NO-SCROLL TREND GROWS: PUT IT AWAY OR ELSE The goal is "to bring back a little slice of human connection that we all feel has been lost with technology," Adam Horner, Antagonist's general manager, told the outlet. The Saloon, a Washington, D.C., bar with no televisions, prohibits phone use altogether. A regular told the Journal the policy pushes back against a bar culture that has become "very insular and not very fun" because of phones. Eulalie, a bistro in Manhattan, states its no-phone policy at the entrance and on its handwritten menus. Co-owner Tina Vaughn told the Journal that diners welcome it. MORE AMERICANS ARE DINING ALONE AS SOLO RESTAURANT RESERVATIONS SOAR, DATA SHOWS "People want an excuse," she said. "They're dying for someone to say, 'You can get off that. It’s OK.'" Philadelphia's Hop Sing Laundromat also bans calls, texting, photos and selfies as part of its tightly controlled speakeasy experience, according to reports, and guests are briefed on the rules upon arrival. Other spots, meanwhile, are taking a more subtle approach. The Edge Harlem in New York City does not offer Wi-Fi and displays a sign on the bar that says, "No Wi-Fi. No Screens. Connect With Each Other," the Journal reported. RESTAURANT OWNER SAYS DINING ROOM IS 'NOT A PLAYGROUND' AS ETIQUETTE EXPERTS WEIGH IN ON VIRAL DEBATE Across the Atlantic, restaurants are trying different approaches, according to The Guardian. Spy Bar in London places stickers over phone camera lenses, while AI Condominio in Verona, Italy, offers diners a free bottle of wine if patrons hand over their phones before eating. The practice appears most common at curated, higher-end experiences such as tasting-menu restaurants, cocktail lounges and listening bars, Fox News Digital previously reported, but even some major chains are experimenting with phone limitations. Chick-fil-A offers a "Cellphone Coops Challenge" at select locations, so groups can stash their phones in a box while they eat in exchange for free ice cream. AMERICANS ARE PAYING PEOPLE TO WAIT IN LINE FOR TIKTOK-FAMOUS FOOD The movement comes as phones have become as common as place settings, with people snapping food photos, taking videos, making loud calls and scrolling through social media during meals. Phones can disrupt the carefully timed rhythm of service, especially when a drink or dish is meant to be served at a certain temperature or with an explanation, Sanwar Mal Khokhar, a Dallas-based mixologist and beverage program leader, told Fox News Digital. Flash photography, filming that blocks service areas and recording nearby diners without regard for privacy can affect both staff and other guests, he added. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Still, a universal phone ban would go too far, Khokhar said. "Taking a quick photo of the drink or food is fine, checking a message is alright or looking up an unknown ingredient is OK," Khokhar said. "All these things are, I think, part of modern life." Rather than confiscating devices, he suggested voluntary phone-free events, screen-free sections or a small surprise from the kitchen or bar for guests who choose to participate. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Rachael Barclay, founder of Seattle-based Vantage and former general manager of the Columbia Tower Club, said that while "there's something to phones being the new cigarette," their overuse is "a societal problem, not a restaurant problem." "A locked pouch is the opposite of hospitality." Barclay also said frequent phone calls are an "operations problem" that better pacing, engaging service and a more inviting table experience could fix. articles.title: Self-defence or safer spaces? What recent assaults say about how we approach women’s safety
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A Class X girl returning from coaching with a friend on a scooter being stopped by a group of youths on a public road.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A Class X girl returning from coaching with a friend on a scooter being stopped by a group of youths on a public road. A 17-year-old at a Delhi park, separated from her male friend by men ‘posing as policemen’. A 16-year-old stranded in the rain who boarded a bus after its driver and conductor ‘offered to take her towards her destination’.In recent weeks, a series of assault cases involving girls and women in public spaces, transport and other everyday settings has again brought an old response into focus: learn to protect yourself.For many women, the immediate response is not to wait for the next security measure but to change something about themselves: the route, the timing, the people they travel with, or what they carry.But there is another side to that conversation. If women are expected to be more alert, learn self-defence and change the way they travel, what happens to the spaces they are expected to navigate every day?‘Taught this since childhood’Delhi reported 13,396 cases of crime against women, including 1,058 cases of rape in 2024. The capital also registered 7,662 crimes against children in 2024. Delhi Police said the city recorded 1,901 rape cases in 2025 as against 2,076 in 2024 and 2,141 in 2023.For some women, the advice to be more careful after every assault is hardly new.“As a woman in this country, I don’t think we needed any more cases to change the way we travel,” said Siddhi.“We have been taught since childhood how to travel, how to ‘be safe’ and how to protect ourselves, all so that we don’t become the next target of sexual assault,” she said.Her interest in martial arts, however, did not begin because of safety concerns. It came from watching international competitions.That distinction is central to the debate. Learning a combat sport can be a choice. It could be for fitness, competition, confidence or simply interest. Turning it into a safety requirement is a different proposition.Laxmi, who has become more conscious about the timings and routes she takes, said she now keeps her phone accessible and remains more alert in unfamiliar surroundings. But she does not want fear to dictate how she lives.She does not believe women should have to take responsibility for someone else’s decision to harm them.“I would choose a safer environment because we as human beings obviously want the freedom to move around without constantly having to think about protecting ourselves,” she said, describing self-defence as an “added strength” rather than a necessity.For others, training offers precisely that sense of added preparedness.Asmita, who trains in MMA, distinguishes between feeling safer and feeling more prepared. Self-defence can give a person greater control in an unsafe situation, she said, but that does not make the environment itself safer for everyone.Unnati, meanwhile, carries pepper spray even on her hostel-to-college commute. She said she has considered self-defence partly because of her parents and sees it as something that can help in the immediate moment, even while questioning whether it can be a long-term answer.What martial arts can and cannot prepare you forThe distinction becomes important when martial arts training is brought into the conversation as a response to assault.Avinash Pandey, a coach at Game Changers Martial Arts Academy, trains children in taekwondo, MMA and self-defence. He said regular martial-arts training develops more than the ability to fight.He pointed to discipline, coordination, reflexes, concentration, confidence and the ability to remain controlled under pressure. Training can also improve confidence and help children overcome fear and bullying.Children can begin at around five, provided they can understand and follow instructions, he said.But competitive martial arts and an actual assault are different situations.A formal competition is conducted within rules and under controlled conditions. A real-life assault does not follow either.A real attack can involve surprise, several people, a weapon, a confined space or a situation in which the person being attacked has little time to react. Self-defence training can give someone skills and confidence, but it cannot guarantee that a person will be able to overpower an attacker or escape every situation.Pandey said recent assault cases have led to more enquiries and enrolments. But he also sees a larger problem in the fact that people often turn to self-defence as a reaction to the latest case of assault/harassment/bullying.“The main responsibility lies with the government, people residing there and society to make the area/place safe for everyone to use,” he said. “Self-defence is secondary, making the places safe comes first.”When the space itself becomes part of the problemThe recent Kalkaji case puts that distinction into sharper focus.A 17-year-old girl was allegedly gang-raped in Aastha Kunj Park near Kalkaji Mandir after three men allegedly posed as policemen, separated her from her male friend and took her to a secluded part of the park.The incident prompted the Delhi Development Authority (DDA) to order a safety audit of parks, with measures including additional lighting and floodlights, CCTV at entry gates, evening vigilance, more security personnel at vulnerable points, controlled access after sunset and identification of dark spots.TOI's reporting from Aastha Kunj also found multiple access points, poorly lit stretches and gaps in security at the park.The response shifts the question away from what the girl could have done differently and towards what the space itself was offering, or failing to offer, in terms of visibility, surveillance and access to help.The same question appears in other recent cases, although the circumstances are different.In Jamui, the Class X girl was allegedly surrounded by a group of youths while returning from coaching. Police said the incident lasted around 20 minutes, with only parts of it captured in two videos that later surfaced online.The videos helped investigators trace the victims, after which an FIR was registered under the POCSO Act and relevant provisions of the BNS. Three people have been arrested so far, police said.In Samastipur, another video showed a young woman allegedly being surrounded and harassed by a group near an embankment after she and a male acquaintance stopped there to take photographs. Police registered a suo motu FIR and arrested all four accused.In both cases, the incidents unfolded in open public spaces. The question is not simply whether the person being targeted knew how to fight back. It is also whether there were people, surveillance, policing or other safeguards around them that could have interrupted the situation.And when the victim is a child, the limits of putting that responsibility on the individual become even clearer.A three-year-old cannot be expected to recognise an unsafe person, assess an escape route or use a self-defence technique.In one recent Delhi case, a three-year-old nursery student was allegedly sexually assaulted by a school cab driver who had worked at the school for around eight months.Police said the accused allegedly lured the child with chocolates and CCTV footage helped identify him. His phone was also reportedly found to contain videos of him offering chocolates to other children.In another Delhi case, a three-and-a-half-year-old boy was allegedly physically and sexually assaulted at a private playschool in Maujpur. CCTV footage purportedly showed the child being tied to a chair, kicked and held by his ears.Police booked the school director, principal, teacher and caretaker under the POCSO Act and the BNS, while the directorate of education ordered an inquiry.Here, the question of whether a child should know self-defence almost becomes irrelevant. The child is inside a space where adults and institutions are expected to provide supervision and protection.The same applies to the journey to and from those spaces.When safety depends on the system around youIn the moving-bus case, the 16-year-old Class XI student had not set out looking for an unsafe situation. She had got off at the wrong stop amid heavy rain and darkness and was trying to find a way towards her destination when the driver and conductor of a sleeper bus allegedly offered to take her towards Noida Sector 63. She was later allegedly raped inside the moving bus and abandoned near Kashmere Gate.The Supreme Court on Monday drew a parallel with the 2012 Nirbhaya case and took suo motu cognisance of this issue.It also expressed “anguish and deep concern” over recent rape cases in Delhi-NCR and said such incidents point to a systematic failure of law enforcement and public administrative authorities to ensure basic public safety.The moving-bus case exposed questions that self-defence training cannot answer: who is allowed to operate a passenger vehicle, who is inside it, whether a passenger can summon help and whether surveillance systems actually work when something goes wrong.TOI’s reporting found gaps including defunct CCTV and the absence of stops along the route. The National Human Rights Commission subsequently sought reports from the Delhi and Gautam Buddh Nagar police commissioners on the investigation and measures taken in the case.The setting is different from a park, but the problem is similar. A person can be alert and still be dependent on the people and systems around them.That dependence becomes even more pronounced for children travelling to school.The NCPCR’s guidelines on preventing bullying and cyberbullying, for instance, recommend measures such as staff accompanying students on school buses, training staff to identify bullying, providing children with numbers they can use to seek help and installing CCTV in playgrounds and buses.These are not measures a child can put in place alone.Ishita said she has become increasingly conscious about how and where she travels, sharing her live location with friends even on short rides and constantly paying attention to who is around her.“It’s tiring, to be honest.” She said the habit was not something she consciously decided to adopt but something that happened “after every new case” she read about.She has also started watching self-defence videos that appear on her social media feed, even though she has not formally learnt the techniques.But her reaction to the advice that women should learn self-defence is less about rejecting the training and more about what happens when it becomes the only response.“It’s not wrong advice exactly, learning to defend yourself isn’t a bad thing but when it’s the only advice given after an assault, it shifts the conversation from ‘why did he do this’ to ‘what could she have done differently’,” she said.For her, the answer lies in the surroundings.“Self-defence helps me in one moment, against one person. A safer environment protects me and every other woman all the time,” she said.Beyond the latest casePandey reiterated that the two things need not compete: martial arts can teach a child discipline, confidence and the ability to respond under pressure, while self-defence can give an individual another tool when something goes wrong.But the responsibility for preventing an assault cannot sit with the person who may be targeted.A safer park does not require every woman entering it to know how to fight. A properly monitored school bus does not require a child to know how to escape an attacker. A school with functioning safeguards does not expect a three-year-old to recognise danger.The students of DU’s Lady Shri Ram College, marching after a police encounter near their back gate, were asking for something that goes beyond another list of precautions: safer routes, reliable last-mile connectivity, visible police presence, functioning lighting and clear reporting mechanisms.In the world’s largest democracy, the freedom to move without constantly calculating risk should not have to be treated as an individual skill, or something women have to train themselves for. If women must learn to fight back, who is making sure they don’t have to?You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.title: Palestinians denounce Israeli minister Ben-Gvir’s threats against prisoner
articles.summary: Footage of national security minister taunting Hassan Salama in his cell draws sharp condemnation from Palestinians.
articles.body:
The Palestinian Commission of Detainees and Ex-Detainees Affairs has condemned far-right Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir after he posted footage on social media showing him telling jailed Hamas figure Hassan Salama in his cell that he wanted to kill him.

“The footage published by Ben-Gvir shows that degradation and depravity have reached their highest levels,” Raed Abu al-Hummus, the head of the Palestinian Authority agency, said in a statement on Monday.

Conditions inside Israeli prisons are “organised terrorism”, he added.

Ben-Gvir uploaded footage in a lengthy post on X on Sunday showing him inside the cell of Salama, who has been imprisoned by Israel for 30 years.

Salama is serving multiple life sentences for his role in a series of Hamas-orchestrated attacks in 1996, including bus bombings.

“I want to kill you. …. I want you executed,” he told Salama while surrounded by Israeli security forces. According to Ben-Gvir, the video was taken two weeks ago.

The Palestinian Prisoners Media Office called Ben-Gvir’s actions “a cheap political and electoral stunt” made before Israel’s October 27 elections and a “cowardly act of bullying against a defenceless and handcuffed prisoner”, adding that Israeli authorities were fully responsible for Salama’s life.

Palestinian group Hamas said Ben-Gvir’s threat to kill Salama “signals new crimes” against Palestinian detainees, while pledging to continue efforts to secure their release.

Ben-Gvir’s video, in which he also repeated his calls for the execution of Palestinian prisoners, follows other recent incidents in which he has directly threatened Palestinian prisoners, underscoring his record of incendiary rhetoric and hardline policies towards Palestinians held in Israeli prisons.

In August, Ben-Gvir posted a video of himself entering the prison cells of Palestinian women and boasting about their inadequate conditions.

Last year, the minister was seen taunting long-imprisoned Fatah leader Marwan Barghouti in his jail cell.

Israel’s Knesset approved legislation in March allowing the death penalty for Palestinian prisoners in certain cases, a measure strongly backed by Ben-Gvir and his party, Jewish Power. The law does not permit the death penalty for Jewish Israelis.

The legislation drew widespread criticism and protests from countries in the region over its implications for Palestinian prisoners.

Ben-Gvir has previously said Jewish Power would demand the defence and justice portfolios as a condition for joining a future government.

On Sunday, Ben-Gvir also called for the “emigration” of Palestinians from Gaza and the occupied West Bank.

Ben-Gvir in July unveiled a seven-year plan branded “Disengagement 710” to remove Gaza’s roughly two million residents through what he called “voluntary emigration”.

Ben-Gvir added that if re-elected, he would establish a migration ministry to expel Palestinians.

In July, Israeli cabinet members and parliamentarians, including Ben-Gvir, joined a march towards Gaza to call for the rebuilding of Jewish settlements in the besieged Palestinian territory.

The Israeli minister has also pushed plans for annexing much of the occupied Palestinian territory despite condemnation from European and Arab leaders.

This year, Ben-Gvir approved the issuance of gun licences to Israelis in 18 additional settlements in occupied Palestinian territory, which are illegal under international law.

articles.title: Details emerge of suspects in alleged terror plot near UK air base used by US forces – but questions remain
articles.summary: The five men arrested on suspicion of a terrorist plot to attack an airbase in England used by long-range US bombers are all UK nationals, according to British police, but key questions surrounding the alleged plot - in particular the motive - remain unanswered.
articles.body: The five men arrested on suspicion of a terrorist plot to attack an airbase in England used by long-range US bombers are all UK nationals, according to British police, but key questions surrounding the incident – in particular the motive – remain unanswered. The five are residents of London, and are aged between 23 and 25, according to a statement from counter-terrorism police, which spoke of “multiple new lines of enquiry.” The men, who have not been identified, were arrested early Sunday close to the base at Fairford in western England, from where US B-1 bombers have been flying missions against Iran. “This is a hugely complex and large-scale operation,” Vicki Evans, a senior counter-terrorism officer, said on Monday, urging that investigators be “given the space” to get on with their job. UK authorities have not disclosed where the men are being held, nor what was found in three white vans the men appear to have used. Aerial footage on Sunday showed a bomb disposal robot roaming between the vans in woods near the base. The rear doors of two of the vans were open and large black items could be seen scattered on the ground nearby. CNN teams nearby later heard what sounded like two controlled detonations from the direction of the village where the vans were found. Iranian threat Asked if a hostile foreign state could have been behind the incident, British Defense Minister Wes Streeting said on Monday he did not “want to speculate at this stage of the investigation.” In July, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps specifically noted Fairford’s use by US bombers, warning the UK that “any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces.” The Iranian embassy in London issued a statement Monday saying it “categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations published by some British individuals and media outlets attempting to link Iran to arrest of five suspects in the vicinity of RAF Fairford base.” US President Donald Trump called the arrests “fantastic,” saying the US and the UK had the men under investigation for “a long time.” “Working with Britain, it was an amazing job,” Trump told reporters in Chicago. “They were looking to do big damage to our fort and working with the British worked out great.” “We had them under view for a long time, and we got them,” he said. UK authorities have not commented on the US president’s assertion. It’s unclear whether the five men were under surveillance before their arrival in the Fairford area in the early hours of Sunday. “Hooded and masked” Photographs of the men – shirtless with their hands tied behind their backs – appeared in UK media Sunday. They were initially detained under laws on possession of explosives and were later additionally arrested “on suspicion of preparation of a terrorist act,” according to a statement by counter-terrorism police. A local resident said she came across the men when returning home on Saturday night. “Both the driveway and the road were blocked by three white vans,” she said. The resident, who wishes to remain anonymous, told CNN that the vans were parked in a “strange formation” about 100 meters from the base fence. She believed there were more than five men in the group and most had their faces covered. Authorities have not indicated that they are looking for other individuals. Some ran into the field and some towards the neighboring village, she said. She called the emergency services at 1:40 a.m., according to phone records she showed CNN. Within ten or 15 minutes, armed police arrived. “I think it was pure luck that I arrived in the village at a similar time to the vans,” the resident, a farmer, added. Multiple UK media outlets – including the BBC, the Guardian and the Telegraph – reported, citing sources, that the operation was not intelligence-led, suggesting the vigilance of local residents may have played a key role in alerting authorities. Counter-terrorism police said they first received a call “relating to three suspicious vehicles which appeared to be travelling towards the airbase” about an hour before the resident called. Streeting said the resident had “a partial picture” of the situation, adding that the work of the police and the security services “takes place often unsung, unreported, for good reason,” he said. A cordon around the area where the men were detained remains, with a number of people evacuated from their homes. Tightened security Local people told CNN that security around the base had been tightened in recent days, with roadblocks at the entrance. But roads and lanes in the immediate area were still open. The woman who called the police and one other local resident said that during previous conflicts, such as that against Iraq in 2003, there had been heavy security around the base. But security since the Iran conflict began has been less evident, they said. In March, the UK government gave the US Air Force permission to use Fairford to carry ⁠out strikes on Iranian missile sites used to attack ships in the Strait of Hormuz. Days after the IRGC issued its threat against Fairford in July, Iranian media published a video of a group describing themselves as Iranian patriots at the perimeter fence of the base. “This is RAF Fairford on British soil — the place where US military aircraft take off from these very runways to attack our people and our homeland,” one man says, with an Iranian flag hanging on the fence. “We came to stand just a few meters from the nest of hostile aircraft and raise the proud flag of Iran,” the unidentified man says on the video. A US Air Force spokesperson at Fairford – where the 501st ​Combat Support Wing is based – told CNN on Sunday: “For operational security reasons we will not discuss specific force protection measures.” The unit “remains vigilant and will take appropriate actions to ensure the safety and security of our US service ⁠members, civilians, contractors, and their families,” the spokesperson said. CNN’s James Frater contributed to this report.

articles.title: Motorcycle-borne gunmen kill 3 cops in Pakistan's Khyber Pakhtunkhwa
articles.summary: Three traffic police officers were killed and three others injured in a gun attack in Pakistan's Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province on Monday, the Associated
articles.body: Three traffic police officers were killed and three others injured in a gun attack in Pakistan's Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province on Monday, the Associated Press cited police.The attack took place in Wazirabad Bazaar in Tank district when suspected militants on motorcycles opened fire on a vehicle carrying the traffic police.The attackers fled the area after the shooting, local police official Jamshed Khan said.No group has claimed responsibility for the latest attack. Police are likely to suspect the Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), which has carried out several attacks in the region. The TTP is a separate group from Afghanistan’s Taliban but is allied with it.The attack on police officials came two days after 'fidayeen' bomb blast in Dera Ismail Khan city in the same province. The suicide bombing killed at least 13 people and wounded over 30 others.Gunmen also opened fire on an ambulance that arrived at the scene. The TTP claimed responsibility for that attack.Pakistan has repeatedly accused Afghanistan’s Taliban government of allowing TTP militants to operate from Afghan territory and carry out attacks in Pakistan.Kabul has denied the allegations and said it does not allow its territory to be used against other countries.You use AI every day. articles.title: Accused drug lord "The Spider" extradited to U.S. from Colombia
articles.summary: Geovany Andres Rojas, who faces drug trafficking and terrorism charges in the U.S., had been protected from extradition by former Colombian President Gustavo...
articles.body:
A Colombian warlord, whose extradition to the United States had been delayed for several months while he was designated a peace negotiator by the country's previous government, was flown to California and placed in custody of federal agents.

Geovany Andres Rojas faces drug trafficking and terrorism charges in the United States. For years, he acted as a spokesman and leader of Comandos de la Frontera, a rebel group known for trafficking cocaine in Putumayo, a Colombian province that borders Ecuador and Peru.

Rojas, who is also known as "Araña" ("The Spider"), had been protected from extradition by former Colombian President Gustavo Petro, who had asked him to participate in peace talks with the Colombian government.

But a new government, led by conservative President Abelardo de la Espriella, lifted the ban on Rojas's extradition, signaling a shift in the nation's security strategy.

"You don't build peace by protecting narco-terrorists like this bandit," De la Espriella said on Friday, after he personally supervised Rojas' transfer to the U.S. "I ask U.S. authorities … that he cannot negotiate deals that will leave his crimes unpunished."

The U.S. Justice Department released a photo of Rojas flanked by law enforcement after being extradited to the United States.

"Colombia and the Department of Justice are making a clean sweep of narcoterrorists, starting with Araña," U.S. Attorney Adam Gordon said in a statement .

Rojas was arrested in Bogota in February 2025, and Colombia's Supreme Court approved his extradition to the U.S. in October. But Petro suspended it, arguing he needed Rojas to participate in peace talks between the Colombian government and several rebel groups, including Comandos de la Frontera.

De la Espriella, who was elected in June, has suspended talks with rebel groups and has taken an iron-fist approach to crime. It recently included militarizing a city in the north of Colombia, where a drug gang attempted to impose a three-day curfew. The conservative leader was endorsed by President Donald Trump while campaigning and has said he will work closely with the United States to fight drug trafficking.

Colombia's government has struggled to contain violence in rural areas in recent years, as drug gangs and rebel groups fight over territory abandoned by the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia or FARC, following their 2016 peace deal with the government.

More than 14,000 fighters laid down their weapons as a result of the agreement that ended five decades of guerrilla warfare. But the peace deal also left a power vacuum in regions with little state presence, where illegal activities like the cocaine trade are common. Several breakaway groups are now fighting over drug trafficking routes, illegal mines and extortion rackets in these areas.

Comandos de la Frontera emerged in 2017 and is partly led by former FARC fighters who did not join the 2016 peace deal. The group formed an alliance with the Segunda Marquetalia organization, a group founded in 2019 by former FARC commander Luciano Marin. But the alliance fell apart two years ago, leaving Comandos de la Frontera to conduct separate negotiations with Colombia's government.

Rojas is expected to make his initial court appearance on Monday.

articles.title: Netanyahu made a secret visit to the UAE on Sunday, source says
articles.summary: The trip comes one month before Israel’s elections and against the backdrop of heightened political controversy in Israel over reports that Bin Zayed had warned Netanyahu of a major Hamas operation days before the October 7, 2023, attack.
articles.body: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu secretly visited the United Arab Emirates on Sunday and met with the country’s president, Sheikh Mohammed bin Zayed, an Israeli source familiar with the visit told CNN. The source said Iran dominated the agenda, an arena where the two countries have deepened their cooperation, including during the current Iran war. The Israeli Prime Minister’s Office did not confirm the visit. CNN reached out to the UAE foreign ministry for comment. The rare trip, if confirmed, comes exactly one month before Israel’s October 27 election and against the backdrop of heightened political controversy in Israel over reporting by Haaretz and The New York Times alleging that Bin Zayed had warned Netanyahu of a major Hamas operation days before the October 7, 2023, attack. The Atlantic separately reported that Egypt’s intelligence chief Abbas Kamel flew to Israel on September 26, 2023, to warn that Gaza would “blow up.” And on Sunday, The Wall Street Journal reported that there were at least three Egyptian warnings conveyed to Israel about Gaza, the last one in a phone call to Netanyahu, just days before the attack. Netanyahu’s office has repeatedly denied receiving any warning and has dismissed the reports as fabricated lies aimed at damaging him electorally. But his rivals have used the allegations to make accountability for the failure to prevent the October 7, 2023, attack a central campaign issue. After initial reports of a warning from Bin Zayed, the UAE’s Foreign Ministry said earlier this month that it “does not comment on media stories or speculation regarding conversations between government leaders,” but it did not deny the call. “When necessary, all relevant intelligence has been and continues to be communicated between the relevant entities,” the statement said. At the time, an Israeli source familiar with the matter said Netanyahu’s office tried to get the UAE to deny the report, but the UAE only agreed to issue a statement about intelligence sharing. Netanyahu’s Likud party subsequently issued a statement, posted on the prime minister’s X account, alleging “blatant foreign interference” in Israel’s elections by UAE-based Palestinian politician Mohammed Dahlan. The party provided no evidence for the claim. Netanyahu’s rivals, meanwhile, have seized on the reported warning to renew their attacks on his handling of the events preceding October 7. Gadi Eizenkot, currently polling as the prime minister’s main challenger in Israel’s upcoming elections, said Saturday that the revelation about the warning “leaves no room for doubt: Netanyahu led, with blindness, arrogance and irresponsibility, the State of Israel to the greatest disaster in its history.” In May, Netanyahu’s office said the prime minister had secretly visited the UAE in March, during the early days of the Iran war, calling it a “historic breakthrough.” The UAE foreign ministry, however, denied his claim at the time as “completely unfounded.” During the war, Israel is also said to have deployed an Iron Dome missile defense system to the UAE and Israeli officials have said security cooperation between the two countries reached unprecedented levels. Netanyahu has never made a publicly acknowledged official visit to the UAE.

articles.title: AAP donations drop 68%; firm founded by ex-MP who joined BJP had given Rs 5 cr of 12.10 cr
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Arvind Kejriwal-led Aam Aadmi Party received Rs 12.10 crore in contributions in 2025-26, a 68% drop from the previous financial year,
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Arvind Kejriwal-led Aam Aadmi Party received Rs 12.10 crore in contributions in 2025-26, a 68% drop from the previous financial year, according to its latest report filed with the Election Commission.Nearly 83% of the party's contributions came from two donors, Prudent Electoral Trust and Trident Limited. Both gave Rs 5 crore each. Trident was founded by former AAP Rajya Sabha member Rajinder Gupta.The remaining contributions amounted to around Rs 2.10 crore, according to the report.Gupta was elected to the Rajya Sabha on an AAP ticket in October 2025. Trident's Rs 5-crore cheque was dated January 9, 2026, when Gupta was still with the AAP.He joined the BJP after Raghav Chadha led rebellion, merging two-third of AAP's Rajya Sabha strength into the ruling saffron party in April this year.The AAP had reported contributions of Rs 38.10 crore in 2024-25, compared with Rs 11.06 crore in 2023-24. Prudent Electoral Trust was the party's biggest donor that year, contributing Rs 16.40 crore.The latest filing covers the first full financial year after the AAP lost power in Delhi in February 2025. The party continues to govern Punjab, where Trident is based.The AAP report has 1,202 numbered entries. Punjab AAP president Aman Arora is listed against 12 payments of Rs 10,000 each, adding up to Rs 1.20 lakh.How other regional parties faredThe latest filings of other regional parties also show a decline in contributions compared with 2024-25.The Telugu Desam Party (TDP), which came to power in Andhra Pradesh, reported Rs 58.25 crore in contributions in 2025-26, down from Rs 83.03 crore the previous year. Prudent Electoral Trust was its biggest donor, giving Rs 45 crore, compared with Rs 40 crore in 2024-25.The YSR Congress Party (YSRCP), which lost power in Andhra Pradesh to the TDP, reported contributions of Rs 24.31 crore. This was sharply lower than the Rs 140.04 crore it reported in 2024-25. Its biggest donor in the latest filing was Goodwood Sanctuary Private Limited, which contributed Rs 10 crore.The Biju Janata Dal (BJD), which lost power in Odisha in 2024, did not report any contribution above Rs 20,000 in its latest filing. The party had reported Rs 60 crore in 2024-25, all of it received in April and May 2024, before the election results.The BJD had also reported no such contributions in 2022-23 and 2023-24, when electoral bonds were still available.Under the rules, political parties have to disclose the names of donors who contribute more than Rs 20,000 in a financial year.However, these contribution reports do not represent a party's total annual income, which is disclosed separately in its audited accounts.Get the latest India News and Live updates.
