articles.title: Ethiopia accuses Sudan, Egypt of backing Tigray rebels as fighting rages
articles.summary: Sudan army denies backing Tigray fighters, says rival paramilitary RSF receiving support from within Ethiopia.
articles.body:
Ethiopia’s army commander has accused Sudan and Egypt of backing armed groups fighting its troops in the north of the country after heavy clashes resumed between the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) and the federal government.

Speaking on the army’s YouTube channel on Sunday, Field Marshal Birhanu Jula said it was “fighting forces that are organised and allied to serve the interests of external forces”.

He added that these forces would not be able to achieve any gains unless they were “backed, supported and supplied by Sudan, Egypt and other external powers”.

The Sudanese military denied the allegations in a statement on Sunday, calling them “baseless”.

The military, which has been fighting a civil war in Sudan against the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) since 2023, also made a counterclaim, alleging that the RSF was receiving support from within Ethiopia’s territory, including training, supplies and military activity involving drones.

Fighting between the TPLF and Ethiopia’s federal government, led by Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, resumed on Wednesday, raising fears of a return to the 2020-2022 civil war , in which an estimated 600,000 people died.

The headquarters of Tigrai TV, seen as the key outlet for the rebel authorities in the Tigrayan capital, Mekelle, was hit by a drone on Sunday.

Al Jazeera’s Malcolm Webb, reporting from the Kenyan capital, Nairobi, said Ethiopia’s government last week said the station’s operations had been suspended indefinitely.

“The federal government hasn’t commented on this drone strike, but it comes following a significant communications disruption in the Tigray region,” Webb reported.

Communications have been limited since Friday when telecommunications providers reported major disruptions to phone and internet services in Tigray, making reporting on the conflict difficult.

“We don’t know who’s causing this communications blackout, if it’s the federal government repeating its strategies from the last civil war or if it’s TPLF who are trying to prevent electronic communications being used by the federal government to target its drone strikes,” Webb added.

United Nations chief Antonio Guterres’s spokesman said the secretary-general was “particularly troubled by reports of the use of drones as well as incidents of harm to civilians”. No exact figures on the number of casualties were confirmed.

The TPLF has seized airports and launched attacks into the neighbouring states of Afar and Amhara, saying it was engaged in a “defensive war” against the government.

A source told Al Jazeera Arabic that the Ethiopian army has seized control of the city of Alamata in southern Tigray and was advancing towards Mekhoni and Maychew, deeper into the region.

According to the AFP news agency, TPLF fighters took control of the town of Erebti in the Afar region near the border with Tigray on Sunday. The rebels were advancing towards Afdera, a town about 100km (60 miles) to the east, it said.

The TPLF, which has allied with six other armed groups around the country, appeared to be repeating a strategy from the last war of pushing towards Addis Ababa. The offensive in Afar aims to cut off supply lines from Djibouti, the source of the majority of Ethiopia’s imports, including fuel.

The alliance was announced last week and is aimed at overthrowing Abiy’s government.

The formation of the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival brought together longstanding enemies who fought on opposite sides of the 2020-2022 civil war.

articles.title: Offshore wind plant to bring jobs boost to Montrose
articles.summary: The new facility will manufacture parts for offshore wind farms in Scottish waters and for overseas markets.
articles.body:
An offshore wind turbine facility is to be created at the Port of Montrose, supporting about 80 jobs.

The factory, which will make components for off-shore wind turbines, is to be run by engineering firm Subsea Micropiles following a £5m investment.

A further £6.7m is being provided by the state-owned Scottish National Investment Bank, with Scottish Enterprise also pledging £1.45m.

First Minister John Swinney, during a visit to the site in Angus, said it would help ensure "benefits of the energy transition are retained in Scotland".

He also welcomed an announcement from SSE that the Port of Montrose is its preferred location for an operations base for the Berwick Bank B offshore wind farm , which is expected to create a further 100 jobs.

The Berwick project, set to be one of the largest offshore wind farms in the world, will see up to 307 turbines generating enough electricity to power up to six million homes.

Scotland 'at the forefront' of offshore energy

Subsea Micropiles, which has offices in Ireland and Aberdeenshire, already has an operations base at the Port of Montrose.

The firm's new facility is expected to make parts for wind turbines in Scottish waters, and for international markets.

Chief executive Derek Robertson said: "Scotland has become an important base for our growth.

"We rely on the deep pool of talent, skills and offshore experience here to develop our technology, services and expand into a global market.

He added that the company's products "can be manufactured locally, with the potential to retain significant economic benefit in Scotland through engineering, vessel services and offshore supply chain".

Swinney said: "Scotland is already recognised as being at the forefront of floating offshore wind development.

"The investment behind today's announcements is a strong vote of confidence in the sector and in the skilled workforce, innovation and expertise that exists here.

"Subsea Micropiles' commitment to expand at the Port of Montrose will help ensure more of the economic benefits of the energy transition are retained in Scotland, creating high-quality jobs in Angus and the North East, supporting local businesses and strengthening our industrial capabilities."

He added that SSE's selection of Montrose as its preferred location for the Berwick project would strengthen "Scotland's offshore wind supply chain" and create "more jobs as well as investment in skills, infrastructure and local communities".

Contract secured for one of world's largest offshore wind farms

articles.title: Plot 'exposed' by 999 call, 5 men in mid-twenties arrested: What happened near US-run RAF base in UK
articles.summary: Five men were arrested near RAF Fairford in western England on Sunday after police received reports of three suspicious vans travelling towards the
articles.body: Five men were arrested near RAF Fairford in western England on Sunday after police received reports of three suspicious vans travelling towards the military air base, which has been used by US bombers during the war against Iran. The men were initially detained under explosives legislation and were later arrested on suspicion of preparing an act of terrorism. Three vans were searched by an Army bomb-disposal team, while a 400-metre cordon was imposed around the vehicles and residents of about 85 homes in nearby Whelford were evacuated.British counterterrorism officers are now investigating what the men were allegedly planning. No motive has been officially confirmed. The arrests come amid heightened concern in Britain over hostile-state activity and at a particularly sensitive time for RAF Fairford, given its role in US military operations against Iran.5 arrestedFive men were arrested near RAF Fairford in western England early Sunday after police received reports of three suspicious white vans travelling towards the military air base. Gloucestershire Police said the alert came at about 12.45am, prompting armed officers to respond in the Whelford area.The men, all British nationals living in London and in their mid-twenties, were initially arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and later on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act, said the police. The Counter Terrorism Police said they were working to establish the circumstances surrounding the men's activity, their knowledge and any possible motive. "At this time, we are working to establish the full circumstances of the activity of those arrested, their knowledge and any motivation behind this incident," police said. The force also urged caution over speculation about the motive, saying counter-terrorism officers needed "the space to work carefully and clearly."'999 call foiled plans'Police were alerted in the early hours of Sunday after reports of three white vans apparently travelling towards RAF Fairford. A local farmer later told the BBC that she encountered the vans and then saw a group of “hooded and masked men” moving towards nearby fields. She said she called 999 at about 1.36am after initially trying to contact Ministry of Defence police.“I believe that my 999 call foiled whatever plans they had,” the farmer told the BBC. She said armed police arrived in the village within about 10 minutes. Five men were arrested in the Whelford area and were initially held on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act. They were subsequently arrested on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act. The farmer questioned whether the area around the base was being adequately monitored, but Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said she had only a “partial picture” of the incident.Read more: 5 held in UK for suspected plot to attack air base used by USIncident under probeBritish authorities have not publicly established who, if anyone, was behind the suspected plot. However, Reuters reported that investigators were giving greatest weight to a possible Iranian link, while also examining Russian sabotage and an Islamist plot. The investigation comes against a backdrop of repeated British warnings about hostile activity linked to Iran.The timing is significant because RAF Fairford has been used by the US Air Force during its military campaign against Iran. Britain allowed the US to use bases in the UK for what it described as defensive operations against Iranian missiles and their launch sites. Iran has previously warned that bases used to launch attacks against its territory could be considered legitimate targets. British officials have also accused Iran-linked proxies of involvement in arson and sabotage attempts in the UK and elsewhere, allegations Tehran has denied.However, Iran’s embassy in London on Monday denied any involvement. It said in a statement that it “categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations” surrounding the arrest of five men near the base in western England.Bomb-disposal robot usedThe three suspicious vans became the focus of a major security operation after the arrests. Police established a 400-metre cordon around the vehicles and called in the Army's explosive ordnance disposal unit. A bomb-disposal robot was deployed to examine the vans remotely, with footage showing the machine moving around the vehicles and appearing to inspect one of them.Read more: UK police robot targets vans near airbase used by US forcesAbout 85 homes in Whelford were evacuated as a precaution, and residents remained away from their homes on Monday as the investigation continued. Police said the immediate incident appeared to be contained. Security was also tightened around the air base, with heavy vehicles used to block access points and armed officers seen around the main entrance. Authorities have not publicly disclosed what, if anything, was found inside the vans, or whether the vehicles contained functioning explosives.Trump reactsUS President Donald Trump said the suspects had been under investigation by British and US authorities before their arrest and suggested they had been planning a serious attack on the base. “They were looking to do big damage,” Trump told reporters in Chicago on Sunday. He also said, “We had them under view for a long time, and we got them.”Trump said cooperation between the US and Britain had helped lead to the arrests. When asked about a possible Iran connection, he indicated that there was one, although British authorities have not publicly confirmed this as the motive. UK officials have been more cautious because the investigation is still underway. Streeting declined to speculate about the suspects' motives, saying authorities would provide information “as and when we can” without compromising the investigation.Trump hails arrests in UK near US air base over terror suspicionWhy RAF Fairford mattersRAF Fairford is a UK-owned military base operated by the US Air Force under a long-standing arrangement dating back to the Cold War. Located about 160km west of London, it has a runway capable of handling heavy bombers and has been used by US aircraft during major military operations, including the Gulf War and the 2003 Iraq war.The base has taken on renewed importance during the current Iran conflict. US B-1 and B-52 bombers have operated from Fairford during the campaign. It also hosts the headquarters of the US Air Force's 501st Combat Support Wing and the 420th Air Base Squadron. The base has been the target of anti-war protests since the conflict began, but investigators have not said whether the latest incident is connected to protest activity.Situation nowThe five suspects remain in custody while counterterrorism officers investigate the circumstances surrounding their arrest, the contents of the vans and any possible links to a wider plot. Under Britain's terrorism laws, suspects can be detained for up to 14 days before they must be charged or released.Police have not released the men's identities, nationalities or details of any alleged target. The investigation will also have to establish whether there was an organised plan, who may have directed it and whether the suspects had access to explosives capable of causing damage. US military personnel at Fairford have been placed on heightened vigilance, while the US Embassy in London advised Americans in Britain to “exercise caution”.You use AI every day. articles.title: Judge imposes £100,000 bail condition on Rwanda genocide accused
articles.summary: Brown is accused of "killing, directing or encouraging" the deaths of members of the Tutsi ethnic group in Rwanda. He denies wrongdoing.
articles.body:
A man accused of offences relating to the 1994 Rwanda genocide will remain in custody unless he pays the court a £100,000 guarantee.

Dr Vincent Brown, formerly Dr Vincent Bajinya, 65, was allegedly a "leader" or "supervisor" of violent acts carried out by others and is the first person in the UK to be charged over the genocide.

At the Old Bailey on Monday, Judge Mark Lucraft KC granted conditional bail with stricter conditions than at a previous hearing, including the increased surety and electronic monitoring.

Brown is accused of "killing, directing or encouraging" the deaths of members of the Tutsi ethnic group in Rwanda. He denies wrongdoing.

Three members of the same house were allegedly murdered, along with a taxi driver, a mother and her young son between April 6 and 13.

The alleged victims were Dominique Mukurarinda, Immaculee Mukankusi, Gerasi Rurangirwa, Leandre Mbogoye, Charlotte Kamaguja and Olivier Tuyishime.

Brown, of Islington, north London, was charged following a seven-year British investigation into the killings.

An estimated 800,000 Tutsis and politically moderate Hutus were killed during the 1994 Rwanda genocide which lasted for 100 days.

On Wednesday the judge imposed a £100,000 bail condition on Brown's release. This is up from an earlier £25,000 security imposed by magistrates.

Brown was also ordered to surrender his passport and any national identity cards, not to apply for international travel documents and was told he must abide by a curfew to live and sleep at his London address.

He would also be electronically monitored and have to report daily to police.

Lucraft said that until the £100,000 condition was met, the defendant would remain in custody.

Brown is a medical doctor who qualified in Rwanda in the 1980s. He later became head of the country's Department of Family Health in Kigali and lived in a suburb there with his wife and young son.

In 2006 he was worked at Praxis, a London-based charity which helps refugees from places like Rwanda.

He has also served on the Refugee Nurses Task Force, which was set up in 2003 to advise the UK government.

Brown is next due to appear at the Old Bailey on 9 October.

Inquiries continue into other alleged genocide offences in Rwanda.

articles.title: From mountain guns to missiles and drones: How India's artillery evolved over nearly 200 years
articles.summary: In the wee hours of May 7, 2025, the stillness and silence of the night was broken by the big guns of the Indian artillery.
articles.body: In the wee hours of May 7, 2025, the stillness and silence of the night was broken by the big guns of the Indian artillery. Although the attacks on the terror nerve centres at Muridke and Bahawalpur stole the headlines, the Army had struck seven more targets across both the Line of Control and the international border.These targets were hit by precision fire from artillery guns and loitering munitions. The message was clear: there was no safe space on the other side of the border.The pinpoint dropping of munitions on these terror targets was the latest feat in a long and storied history of the artillery arm, which now has nearly 200 years of service under its belt.The importance of long-range firepower in a non-contact but kinetic conflict has grown in the last few years, as demonstrated first in Ukraine and then reiterated by Iran. The Americans, too, have shown their dependence on long-range vectors such as the Tomahawk cruise missile and the PrSM to degrade adversarial air defences before sending in aircraft for stand-in attacks.India, which is unlikely to be inducting stealth aircraft in the near future, is more likely to depend on stand-off weapons in the initial phases of a conflict, as was demonstrated during Operation Sindoor. Artillery’s unique capability to “strike deep and strike hard” is therefore even more important for the country.From Panipat to Mysorean rockets: India's long artillery traditionThe Regiment of Artillery has, from its first use in the sub-continent during the mid-14th century Bahmani-Vijayanagar War, only grown in significance. In the Battle of Panipat in 1526, artillery was decisively used to defeat the much larger Delhi Sultanate army of Ibrahim Lodhi, thus laying the foundation of the Mughal Empire. Though the artillery arm of the Marathas was weaker than many of their contemporaries, Balaji Baji Rao organised the arm on professional lines and Madhavji Sindhia established a fairly efficient gun manufacturing foundry under the supervision of European gun makers.The Indian artillery tradition has left another mark halfway around the world. The American national anthem also gives an ode to the Indian artillery tradition, with the lines “and the rockets’ red glare, the bombs bursting in air, gave proof through the night that our flag was still there”. The red glare of the rockets that features prominently in the US national anthem came from rockets fired by the British at Fort McHenry during the War of 1812. But the British had themselves been at the receiving end of Mysorean rockets and, after the defeat of Tipu Sultan, adapted the technology into what came to be known as the Congreve rocket.The modern Indian ArtilleryThe modern Regiment of Artillery traces its origins to September 28, 1827, when the British East India Company raised 5 (Bombay) Mountain Battery, originally the 8th Company of the Golandaz Battalion, Bombay Foot Artillery. It was the first unit of what would eventually become the Regiment and the first to be manned by native Indian soldiers. Specialising in mountain warfare, it set the template for the versatile artillery units the Army fields today.By the time of Independence, Indian Artillery had grown into a multi-branch arm, comprising Field, Medium, Air Defence, Counter Bombardment, Coastal, Air Observation Post and Survey units. Partition then split the Royal Indian Artillery, with India retaining eighteen and a half regiments while Pakistan received the remaining nine and a half.The Regiment has since fought in all the major conflicts the nation has fought in. In 1947-48, its guns helped hold key positions in the high-altitude terrain of Kashmir. In 1962, despite being outgunned and ill-prepared, artillery units inflicted considerable damage on the enemy. In 1965, its firepower proved decisive against Pakistani armour. In 1971, it provided overwhelming fire support in both the Eastern and Western theatres. During Kargil in 1999, artillery pounded enemy positions along the ridges, aiding the recapture of Tiger Hill and Tololing, with the Bofors guns earning particular praise for their accuracy.The vast majority of artillery regiments are equipped with the indigenous 105 mm Indian Field Gun or the Light Field Gun, while Pinaka, Dhanush and, in the future, the Advanced Towed Artillery Gun System (ATAGS) will increase the indigenous mix of equipment. The arm also has domestically assembled K9 Vajra guns, while the Russian-origin M-46 130mm artillery gun is also being up-gunned to 155mm domestically.The growing importance of artilleryArtillery in the future will encompass a large portion of the battlefield. There won't be a battle without artillery. Due to the nature of the arm it will be involved in long range kinetic operations and choke point operations in all types of terrain. This will have great value as this capability will have huge deterrent capability. But to fully exploit this, we need ground, air and space based sensors. There is a need to think of artillery differently, to make use of upcoming capabilities, the current way of thinking will not let us take full advantage of these systems.Since then, the Regiment of Artillery has grown by leaps and bounds in numbers and capability. The arm is now the second-largest arm of the Army, following the infantry and followed by the mechanised component. In terms of capability, the arm has grown from initially operating guns such as the 3.7-inch mountain gun and the 25-pounder to the 5.5-inch medium artillery gun.Now, the artillery is in the midst of a modernisation drive known as the Field Artillery Rationalisation Plan, which seeks to bring the gun regiments of the artillery to a common calibre of 155mm. This is the same bore as that of the now-famous Bofors gun.The Regiment of Artillery is also extending its reach with rocket systems such as the Pinaka, which is soon expected to reach an operational range of 120 km. The arm also demonstrated the Suryastra rocket system during this year’s Republic Day parade. This weapon system has a range of up to 300 kilometres.Apart from these battlefield weapons, the arm is also the custodian of the country’s tactical and strategic weapons. These range from the BrahMos missile that proved its effectiveness during Operation Sindoor to other weapons, including the Agni and Prithvi series of missiles. Once weapons such as the Long Range Cruise Missile (LRCM), Shaurya and Pralay are inducted, they will also equip the regiment. This means that in any future conflict, artillery will have a central role to play in any shooting conflict.The eyes behind the guns: ISR, drones and the kill chainSurveillance and Target Acquisition (SATA) regiments of artillery, which are tasked with monitoring the adversary’s dispositions, are being armed with Loitering Munitions (LM), thus giving the eyes and ears of the arm a precise manner of punching through the enemy’s defences in a more timely and effective manner. Artillery regiments are expected to deploy an increasing number of drones to keep a tab on enemy movements. Besides existing systems such as electro-optics, weapon locating radars and drones, the arm also requires a constellation of low earth orbit satellites to keep persistent eyes on target.Today, the force rests on two pillars: firepower and Intelligence, Surveillance & Reconnaissance (ISR). Firepower in contemporary warfare is often described through the acronym DRAM, standing for drones, rockets, artillery and missiles. The second pillar, ISR, covers intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance. Without advanced sensors, fast communication and robust networking, firepower is effectively blind.An effective kill chain depends on the seamless pairing of sensor and shooter through secure networks, and the age-old sequence of seeing, acquiring and hitting a target remains a fundamental requirement. Meeting it means integrating space links, electronic warfare capabilities and persistent UAV surveillance so that long-range vectors can strike with precision.What India now needs its artillery to doArtillery is expected to deliver on five broad requirements. The first is conventional deterrence, the promise of overwhelming precision fire that discourages an adversary from embarking on a misadventure. The second is the ability to strike deep, using long-range vectors, both current and futuristic.The third concerns the contact battle. Rocket forces in several other countries operate in silos that do not lend themselves to battlefield synergy, whereas India needs a force that can reinforce the firepower available to frontline troops and provide additional punch from battalion to corps commanders. The fourth requirement is manoeuvre.In seemingly static battlefields, the force must enable manoeuvre or generate what is termed manoeuvre by fire, restoring mobility to a fight that has stalled, as seen in Ukraine. This also includes the idea of horizontal escalation, as witnessed in Iran, where strategic goals can be pursued without direct troop engagement.

articles.title: Man charged with murdering 63-year-old woman in Central Park
articles.summary: A man is under arrest in the killing of a 63-year-old woman inside Central Park, the NYPD said.
articles.body: A man is under arrest in the killing of a 63-year-old woman inside Central Park, the NYPD said late Sunday. Jonathan Robles, 36, was booked for murder and criminal possession of a weapon around 9 p.m. Robles’ last listed address is the Barbour Hotel homeless shelter in Hell’s Kitchen. Investigators said Sunday night that the victim, who was found near East Drive and East 74th Street, had a head trauma. Police retracted an earlier statement that the woman had been stabbed. The NYPD said it received a call about an unconscious woman at around 9:40 a.m., as a slow-moving nor’easter drenched the region. The woman was pronounced dead at the scene. Officials said the woman who died did not have identification. The death left some Central Park visitors shaken. “Terrible. This is our playground. It’s our backyard... it’s the last thing you want to happen,” John, a New York City resident, said. “It’s very terrible and sad news because we are tourists and we expect to pass a good time so it’s very sad,” tourist Guadalupe García said. “I will try to enjoy the park in this time and not at the dark, for example.” Police believe the victim may have been experiencing homelessness.

articles.title: Child, forced marriages of minority girls in Pakistan flagged at UN event
articles.summary: The impact of child and forced marriages on girls in Pakistan, particularly those from minority communities, was discussed at a side event during the 63rd
articles.body: The impact of child and forced marriages on girls in Pakistan, particularly those from minority communities, was discussed at a side event during the 63rd session of the United Nations Human Rights Council in Geneva.Speakers at the event raised concerns about girls being married at a young age and the consequences for their education, health and basic rights. The event was reported by Global Human Rights Defence, a UN ECOSOC-accredited human rights organisation.Naveed Walter, president of Human Rights Focus Pakistan and a human rights defender, pointed to the scale of child rights violations in Pakistan and the vulnerability of children who enter marriage at an early age.“Most recently, UNICEF gave the data about Pakistan. Ninety million women and children and girls have been affected by child rights violations. And of them, 4.8 million were under 15 years of age,” Walter said.Walter said early marriage can leave girls without access to basic education and expose them to serious health risks, particularly during pregnancy.“You know, dear excellencies and dear audience, that during pregnancy, millions of children have died. And you know, under 30 per cent of the children who get married even have basic education,” he said.The discussion also focused on Sindh, where women's rights activist Shagufta Kandhro highlighted the situation of girls who are married before reaching adulthood.“According to the National Commission on the Rights of the Child, 84,000 children between the ages of 10 and 17 are married, widowed and separated. Many of them have already left school, and many face serious health risks,” Kandhro said.Kandhro said 21% of young women in Sindh had been married before turning 18. She also flagged concerns around teenage pregnancies and limited access to maternal healthcare.According to her, Pakistan sees an estimated 61,000 pregnancies among girls aged 15 to 19 each year. Only 44% of pregnant girls in this age group receive at least four antenatal visits, she said.Kandhro also cited anaemia among girls in Sindh, putting the figure at 61.9%. articles.title: Child among three killed off French coast in Channel crossing attempt
articles.summary: France’s maritime police ‌‌said they received a distress call from an inflatable dinghy carrying 105 people.
articles.body:
Three people, including ⁠a child, have died off the coast of France while attempting to cross the English Channel to the United Kingdom, French authorities have said.

France’s maritime police ‌said they had received a distress call from an inflatable dinghy carrying 105 people that ⁠had run into trouble ⁠in calm seas.

The prefecture said the incident involving a “taxi boat” occurred off the coast of Wissant, a seaside village in northern France.

“Taxi boat” refers to a dinghy that approaches the beach from the sea to pick up migrants in shallow waters off the beach.

All passengers on board requested rescue and were taken into care, said the maritime prefecture, adding that the dinghy had not sunk.

The AFP news agency reported that a rescue boat arrived at the port of Calais in mid-morning, where it began disembarking people rescued from the incident.

At least 29 migrants lost their lives last year trying to cross the Channel, according to an AFP tally based on official French and British sources.

More than 41,000 embarked on the dangerous journey across one of the world’s busiest shipping lanes last year.

The issue has been depicted as a crisis by politicians, including Nigel Farage of the far-right party Reform UK, and has been used as a rallying point by anti-immigration activists.

Successive British governments have promised to stop crossings amid organised anti-immigration protests that drew hundreds of demonstrators.

In April, France and the UK signed an agreement to strengthen operations to prevent crossings, with a significant increase in human, technological and intelligence resources.

Last month, a plan put forward by Reform UK to deploy the navy to intercept and return asylum seekers arriving by boat triggered a dispute with France. The French Ministry of the Interior said the measure would breach international law.

articles.title: SpaceX's 'biggest, most powerful' rocket reaches Earth orbit for first time
articles.summary: Elon Musk-led SpaceX’s Starship megarocket reached Earth orbit for the first time on Monday, marking a major milestone for the space company’s ambitious
articles.body: Elon Musk-led SpaceX’s Starship megarocket reached Earth orbit for the first time on Monday, marking a major milestone for the space company’s ambitious plans for the spacecraft.The 407-foot (124-metre) rocket lifted off from SpaceX’s launch site in southern Texas and entered orbit during its latest test flight.The mission was designed to take Starship around Earth six times over nearly 10 hours, flying at an altitude of about 170 miles (275 km), before a planned splashdown in the Pacific Ocean near Chile.Starship, which SpaceX describes as the "biggest and most powerful" rocket ever built, was also carrying 26 of the company’s latest Starlink satellites. The satellites were intended to be deployed in orbit and add to the more than 11,000 Starlink satellites already providing internet services.The uncrewed, 40-storey vehicle consists of a Super Heavy booster topped by the Starship spacecraft. It took off at around 7.46am CT (1246 GMT) from the launch site near Brownsville, along the Gulf of Mexico (Gulf of America).Starship was expected to complete six orbits of Earth during a nearly 10-hour flight before splashing down in the Pacific Ocean west of Chile.Reaching orbit is a key milestone for any rocket designed to carry payloads into space. Starship has yet to achieve the feat despite years of development. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk had earlier predicted that the spacecraft would reach orbit in 2022, followed by satellite deployments in 2023.Since 2023, all 13 previous Starship test flights have remained suborbital, despite nearly a decade of development and more than $15 billion in spending, according to estimates cited in the report.SpaceX plans to use Starship to launch Starlink satellites at a higher frequency and eventually carry astronauts and cargo for Nasa's Moon missions.Musk has also said he wants SpaceX to eventually launch hundreds or even thousands of Starships each year, a scale of operations that would be unprecedented in the space industry.You use AI every day. articles.title: UP eases land-use conversion norms to promote investments in real estate
articles.summary: UP amends land-use conversion rules, letting local development authorities clear plots up to 6,000 sq m with timelines and rationalised charges to boost realty investment.
articles.body: Lucknow: In a major deregulation push aimed at boosting real estate investment, the Uttar Pradesh govt has delegated powers to local development authorities to approve land-use conversion for plots up to 6,000 sq metres, while introducing time-bound clearances and rationalising conversion charges under amended rules notified this month.The amendments to the Uttar Pradesh Urban Planning and Development (Assessment, Levy and Collection of Land Use Conversion Charge) Rules are part of the state’s ease-of-doing-business and deregulation drive. Aimed at speeding up approvals for land-use changes, the revised framework seeks to cut procedural bottlenecks, simplify compliance requirements and support urban development across key growth centres.So far, land-use conversion proposals involved multiple layers of scrutiny and were processed largely through offline procedures. Under the amended framework, development authorities such as Lucknow Development Authority (LDA), Kanpur Development Authority (KDA) and Agra Development Authority (ADA) will be able to handle a significantly larger number of applications locally for plots measuring up to 6,000 sq metres (around 64,600 sq ft), reducing dependence on higher-level approvals and shortening the clearance process.The move is expected to benefit landowners and developers seeking to undertake residential, commercial and mixed-use projects on vacant parcels as well as those pursuing redevelopment initiatives in urban areas. Industry stakeholders believe quicker approvals could improve project viability and reduce holding costs associated with regulatory delays.The govt has also introduced defined timelines to ensure faster disposal of applications. While technical scrutiny will have to be completed within 22 days once the application is submitted, property owners would be granted a time period of 60 days to respond to the queries raised after the technical valuation along with documents. Objections and suggestions to the changes proposed over the land parcel would be decided within 30 days. Once all the formalities are cleared and payment is made to allow land use change, final go ahead would have to be granted within 15 days.Another significant change is the rationalisation of land-use conversion charges. The housing department said the rates were rationalised following a review of practices adopted by other states, with the objective of making Uttar Pradesh more investment-friendly and encouraging faster urban development.Though the amendments were notified on Sept 22, detailed implementation guidelines were recently circulated among development authorities to ensure a smooth transition to the revised system. articles.title: A Pennsylvania family protected a 30-acre farm beside 1,300 acres of preserved land; its mature oaks and hickories now provide habitat for turkeys, bats and hundreds of caterpillar species
articles.summary: A 30-acre farm in Pennsylvania’s Bucks County has been placed under a conservation easement, creating another protected link beside the 55-acre
articles.body: A 30-acre farm in Pennsylvania’s Bucks County has been placed under a conservation easement, creating another protected link beside the 55-acre Russell-Mandel Preserve and a wider network of roughly 1,300 acres of preserved farmland and open space. Heritage Conservancy announced the donation on September 18, while conservation organisation WeConservePA also reported the project on September 24. The property, owned by Leah and Doug Beck, sits in Buckingham Township near the Russell-Mandel Preserve. Rather than allowing the land to become vulnerable to future development, the couple donated a conservation easement to Heritage Conservancy, permanently protecting its natural and agricultural character. The move adds an important piece to an already connected landscape. The nearby Russell-Mandel Preserve itself covers about 55 acres and includes farmland, woodland and a tributary that flows into Pidcock Creek. Heritage Conservancy has described the preserve as part of a broader effort to protect natural and historic resources in Bucks County.Why the trees matterAbout 10 acres of the newly protected property are woodland, much of it made up of mature oak and hickory trees. These forests do far more than provide shade. Native oaks and hickories support insects that form an important part of the food web, while their branches, cavities and dense foliage provide shelter and nesting opportunities for wildlife.According to Heritage Conservancy, the woodland can support animals including wild turkeys and roosting bats, along with hundreds of caterpillar species. The organisation’s assessment also highlights the value of the mature forest for birds that depend on established deciduous woodland.One example is the scarlet tanager, a forest bird associated with mature oak-dominated habitats. Wildlife authorities also recognise the importance of protecting habitat for species facing conservation concerns. Pennsylvania’s current Wildlife Action Plan identifies hundreds of native species as Species of Greatest Conservation Need, a designation used for wildlife facing significant threats, declining populations or other conservation concerns.Farmland adds another layerThe protected landscape is not entirely forested. Around 18 acres of the Beck property consist of pasture and farmland, creating open habitat alongside the wooded areas. That combination can benefit grassland and open-country birds such as the American kestrel and field sparrow. Pennsylvania wildlife monitoring has recorded field sparrows and American kestrels among grassland bird species of conservation interest, highlighting the importance of maintaining suitable open habitats alongside forests.The property’s wooded areas also surround part of a tributary flowing toward Pidcock Creek. Such vegetation along waterways can act as riparian habitat while helping reduce sediment entering streams and supporting water quality.A larger conservation corridorThe significance of the easement extends beyond the 30 acres themselves. Its location next to already protected land means the property becomes part of a larger, connected conservation landscape rather than an isolated patch of habitat. The Russell-Mandel Preserve already supports a variety of wildlife, including turkeys, bats and American kestrels, and contains a native pollinator meadow developed by Heritage Conservancy. The preserve’s meadow and surrounding habitats provide food and shelter for insects, birds and other wildlife.For the Becks, the conservation easement also reflects a long-standing interest in wildlife and land protection. Heritage Conservancy said the couple, who have supported the organisation, have backgrounds surrounded by nature and have volunteered in wildlife rescue.With the easement now in place, the farm will remain part of the area’s protected landscape, preserving woodland, open fields and streamside habitat for wildlife while keeping the land connected to the much larger network around it. The Pennsylvania Wildlife Action Plan similarly emphasises protecting and managing habitat as a way to help at-risk species before they require more intensive intervention.You use AI every day. articles.title: Punjab's election drug debate has old players in new roles: BJP, Congress attack as AAP defends its record
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: \"The sarpanch is also responsible for my death. I had questioned Cheema about drugs. My son takes drugs. My house was sold.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: "The sarpanch is also responsible for my death. I had questioned Cheema about drugs. My son takes drugs. My house was sold. I don't have anything and finally now I have consumed poison. The problem of drugs has not been solved anywhere in Punjab."Those were among the last recorded words of Gulzar Singh, a 47-year-old Dalit man from Dirba in Sangrur district, before his death. His family alleged that he had been pushed to the edge after questioning Punjab finance minister Harpal Singh Cheema about the easy availability of drugs in the area.Gulzar died, but his words reverberated across poll-bound Punjab. The BJP, Congress and Shiromani Akali Dal trained their guns on the Bhagwant Mann government, accusing it of failing to control the drug menace. AAP hit back, questioning their own records in power.Drugs have shadowed election after election in the state. Captain Amarinder Singh went into the 2017 polls promising to break the backbone of the drug trade within four weeks. All the top BJP leaders including Union ministers and party chief ministers from other states have joined the campaign against drugs in Punjab.Yet the BJP has a political history to answer for too. For 10 years, from 2007 to 2017, it shared power with the Shiromani Akali Dal, the period AAP repeatedly points to whenever its record on drugs is questioned.From four weeks to three months: Punjab's many deadlinesAhead of the 2017 election, Amarinder Singh's four-week promise became one of the defining messages of the Congress campaign. He later clarified that his pledge was about breaking the backbone of the drug supply chain rather than completely eliminating every trace of drugs within a month.By 2022, the roles had changed. AAP was the challenger and Arvind Kejriwal and other party leaders promised quick action, speaking of tackling the menace within three to four months of forming the government.The BJP has done its homework well. It knows that the drug menace in Punjab is deep-rooted and hence has sought a timeframe of two years to eradicate it. However, Union minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan has claimed that the BJP will destroy and eliminate the entire drug network within six months if voted to power in the state.Therein lies Punjab's problem: Congress cannot remind AAP about its three-month promise without being reminded of its own four-week vow. BJP cannot attack AAP without being taken back to its decade in government with SAD.Almost every party pointing fingers today has a past of its own to explain.Congress, SAD join the attackThe Congress narrative on the drug menace seems to have been lost in the face of BJP’s high-decibel anti-drug campaign. The party, which for a long time was struggling to set its own house in order amid infighting, has done little till now to capitalise on the alleged failures of the AAP government to tackle the drug menace.The first big Congress show on the ground was only after Sachin Pilot took charge as state incharge and managed to get the rival state unit factions on one stage to protest against Punjab minister Cheema over the suicide of Gulzar.Pilot said: “If someone raises their voice against drugs, they face such attacks. I believe the government can go to any extent to suppress and conceal these voices. There are two sets of laws in the country, one for ministers and another for the common man. This cannot go on. I feel the government is completely on the back foot regarding the issue of drugs.”He then turned to AAP's pre-2022 promise: “The Aam Aadmi Party had promised in Punjab that they would eliminate the drug menace within three months of forming the government. They stand completely exposed. I sense a stir for change in Punjab, and change will happen.”Leader of opposition Partap Singh Bajwa has blamed both the AAP-led state government and the BJP-led Union government for turning the state's drug crisis into a political blame game instead of dismantling the drug supply chain.“Bhagwant Mann cannot wash his hands of responsibility by talking about cross-border, the BSF and Mundra Port. At the same time, the BJP cannot absolve itself by blaming Punjab while the international border, ports and the national drug-trafficking network fall within areas where the Union government has a critical responsibility. Punjab's youth need action, not a Mann-Modi blame-game,” Bajwa said.The Congress challenge is daunting. While on the one hand it has to target the AAP government’s failures, on the other, it also has to prevent the BJP from running away with the anti-drug fight initiative.SAD faces much the same problem. Bikram Singh Majithia recently took a jibe at the Punjab government when he said: “Under AAP's regime, delivery of drugs is faster than that of food.”(function(){function e(){window.addEventListener(`message`,function(e){if(e.data[`datawrapper-height`]!==void 0){var t=document.querySelectorAll(`iframe`);for(var n in e.data[`datawrapper-height`])for(var r=0,i;i=t[r];r++)if(i.contentWindow===e.source){var a=e.data[`datawrapper-height`][n]+`px`;i.style.height=a}}})}e()})();Bathinda MP Harsimrat Kaur Badal has also appealed to women in Punjab to unite and launch an ‘andolan’ to free the state from the drug menace, including through ‘thikri pehra’, a community policing practice in which people guard their localities during emergencies.AAP hits back: What about the years before 2022?AAP's response is to ask its rivals to look backwards before judging the Mann government.Punjab minister Cheema, who is at the centre of the row over Gulzar’s suicide, shifted the blame to the BJP and the SAD.“The BJP should look at its own record. The drug menace intensified during the 10 years of the SAD-BJP government from 2007 to 2017. It was during that period that terms such as 'chitta' and 'smack' became widely associated with Punjab, with countless young lives being destroyed by addiction,” Cheema said.Countering the BJP offensive, AAP national convenor Arvind Kejriwal has alleged that the majority of narcotics entering the country originate from Bharatiya Janata Party-ruled states and major maritime entry points controlled by the Centre.Kejriwal alleged: “Today, 80% of the drugs are coming from BJP-ruled states - Gujarat, Rajasthan, Haryana, UP, Delhi. Has the BJP failed to stop the drug trade in its own states, or does it not want to stop it? Their government has been in power in Gujarat for thirty years, and the highest drug trade is there. Drugs enter India through Mundra Port, and stopping that is the responsibility of the central BJP government.”Bhagwant Mann, meanwhile, has launched the ‘Soorma’ campaign to honour drug-rehabilitated people with specially crafted ‘Soorma’ rings and T-shirts. The chief minister said the initiative aimed to transform recovered drug victims into “Ambassadors of Hope”, who will lead the fight against addiction at the grassroots.Beyond the blame game, what do the numbers say?The Mann government has numbers with which to defend itself.Punjab Police says its ‘Yudh Nashean Virudh’ campaign has resulted in tens of thousands of cases and arrests. More recent state figures put the tally since March 2025 at 61,824 FIRs, 81,433 arrests and 3,918 kg of heroin seized.AAP presents the numbers as evidence that the state machinery is finally going hard after the networks. Its opponents turn the argument around: if such large quantities are still being seized and so many people are still being arrested, how deeply rooted does the trade remain?High seizures can show a crackdown is working but they can also show the scale of the problem being confronted.The government says its strategy now goes beyond policing. It has expanded treatment and rehabilitation under ‘Yudh Nashean Virudh’, with 547 OOAT centres, 219 de-addiction centres and 91 rehabilitation centres, besides programmes involving schools and local communities.For AAP, this forms the other half of its defence: the battle against drugs cannot be measured only through FIRs and seizures but also through treatment and rehabilitation.Punjab has seen this cycle before.In 2017, anger over drugs was directed largely at the SAD-BJP government and Congress promised quick action. By 2022, Congress was on the defensive and AAP used the same issue to argue that Punjab's traditional parties had failed. In 2027, AAP is the incumbent being asked many of the questions it once asked others.The slogans have changed and the roles have reversed, but the question has survived different governments and different deadlines: after so many promises to make Punjab drug-free, why is the state heading into yet another election talking about the same problem?Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: We need to talk about Bandung
articles.summary: In today’s turbulent times, the 1955 conference offers important lessons on global cooperation.
articles.body:
In a world torn apart by geopolitical bullying and geoeconomic warfare, great-power conflict and inequality that concentrates wealth and statecraft in the hands of a few, the Bandung Conference is gaining renewed relevance.

The developing world’s momentous meeting in 1955 laid the groundwork for a new international order and South-South cooperation. It asked a question that everyone, even rich nations, is asking today: who gets to write the rules of the global economy?

That moment needs retelling. In 1955, 29 nations of Asia and Africa, former colonies representing more than half the world, met in Bandung, Indonesia, for a conference hosted by President Sukarno. Riding on the wave of anticolonial struggles, they agreed on an ambitious framework founded on sovereignty and economic, cultural and political cooperation, elevating the United Nations Charter’s spirit of human rights above militaristic alliances.

The conference’s most powerful outcome was South-South solidarity: nations and peoples charting a path independent of the two great powers of that time – the United States and the Soviet Union. As the “Third World” alliance grew, practical efforts to support decolonisation emerged out of it, including the Non-Aligned Movement and bodies like UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD).

As a new Al Jazeera film shows, the “Bandung spirit”, despite efforts not to antagonise great powers, was treated as a direct threat. Many countries faced crushing pushback for committing to the decolonisation agenda – coups, invasions, economic warfare and debt and austerity crises – that left them beholden to old masters, not their development aspirations.

Seventy-one years later, the structures of inequality persist. Despite dramatic growth in parts of the Global South, particularly in East Asia, Global North countries control 69 percent of global wealth while comprising just 20 percent of humanity. Low- and middle-income countries spend on average nearly half their national budgets on debt repayments, mainly to rich creditors in rich countries.

Meanwhile, wealth inequality has soared within nations, concentrating power within small elites while ordinary people struggle. Just 3,000 billionaires hold wealth equivalent to more than 15 percent of global gross domestic product (GDP).

It would be a stretch to suggest that the level of South-South cooperation envisioned at Bandung endures today. The Economist recently quipped, “A damp squib Bandung anniversary shows a lack of solidarity.”

Yet external realities are forcing a reckoning that nostalgia cannot. The powerful are acting with impunity, breaking the brittle cover the so-called rules-based order relied on.

Consider the US-Israel war on Iran – its violence and devastation across the region, and its shock to global fuel and fertiliser prices, punishing common people everywhere.

Consider the wrecking ball of tariffs and its impact on poorer economies, or the profoundly unequal effects as well as drivers of climate breakdown.

Consider the ongoing genocide in Gaza and the impunity afforded to the perpetrators.

The reality is much of the world never accepted the post-World War II order – dominated by powerful nations – as truly legitimate, as the Bandung project demonstrated. But that order did not need to be legitimate to be unavoidable; the alternatives were too costly.

Today, even compliance offers scant security in a world where “might is right”. That is forcing wealthy nations to finally come to terms with what the rest of the world long knew.

Countries must not passively accept these conditions. As Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva put it recently in response to US President Donald Trump’s threat of tariffs: “The world has changed; we do not want an emperor.”

At this time of rupture, the Bandung Conference can offer lessons for rethinking the rules of global cooperation.

First, cooperation alone is value-neutral; the substance matters. More cooperation that advances neoliberal priorities, be it among middle powers or poorer nations, is not the answer.

Second, we need much better institutions. There is an urgent need for serious financial institutions built for the Global South. Alongside this, the IMF and the World Bank should be boldly reformed away from reliance on austerity towards addressing inequality and national sovereignty.

Credit groups such as the Paris Club need to be counterbalanced with borrowers’ clubs of poorer nations. The UNCTAD Borrowers’ Platform, to be launched next month, shows countries can work together to reshape the rules of debt restructuring.

Third, reducing inequality between countries is a partial picture without addressing inequality within and across them. At Bandung, Sukarno warned against “economic control” within nations. Every nation must tackle the consolidation of wealth and power among a tiny few, and boldly reduce the gap between the ultrarich and the rest. Raging against major powers abroad while helping the rich exploit the poor at home does not pass the test of economic liberation.

Fourth, concrete steps are also needed internationally: a negotiation for a fairer international tax system at the UN that ends tax havens and abuses, efforts to tax the ultrarich everywhere and a rewrite of intellectual property rules to prevent corporate monopolies that can come at a devastating human cost.

Fifth, there should also be new trade formations that do not give special powers to foreign investors, and instead focus on advancing workers’ rights and environmental protections. Such forms of South-South cooperation can be vital to addressing the climate crisis.

How cooperation is done matters too. Bandung inspired people across developing and developed countries alike – an internationalist solidarity needed today. Forward-looking policymakers in the Global North have a chance to work constructively – in contrast to the Trump administration’s coercive approach – transforming rules many now admit were rigged.

Spain shows new coalitions are possible on development financing and democracy. The G20 presidencies of Brazil and South Africa have offered hope for multilateralism. An International Panel on Inequality shows new cooperation to address inequality led by the Global South is possible.

Ultimately, the push will come not from leaders but from the people and movements who make them act. Who actually gets to write the rules of the economy? Surely, all of us.
